#6012. Trump highlights NASA nuclear-powered Mars spacecraft mission planned for 2028

President Donald Trump outlined ambitious plans for NASA to launch a nuclear-powered spacecraft to Mars by 2028, return American astronauts to the moon and establish a permanent presence on the lunar surface.

President Donald Trump highlighted NASA's ambitious plans to launch its first nuclear-powered spacecraft to Mars within the next two years, reaffirming his administration's push to expand American space exploration and eventually send astronauts to the red planet.

Speaking at the UP Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida, Trump touted the mission as part of his administration's broader ambitions to expand America's presence beyond Earth.

"Within the next two years, NASA will launch the first-ever nuclear-powered spacecraft to Mars," Trump said.

The president described the mission as a step toward eventually sending American astronauts to the planet.

TRUMP CALLS ISS CREW FROM HOUSTON TO PRAISE SPACE PIONEERS AND OFFER 'OVAL OFFICE TIME'

President Donald Trump highlighted NASA's plans to launch a nuclear-powered spacecraft to Mars within two years during remarks at the UP Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. (Eric Lee/Reuters)

"We're going to be paving the way for astronauts to plant the Stars and Stripes on the red planet," he said.

The planned mission comes as NASA's Artemis program aims to establish a long-term human presence on the moon before eventually sending astronauts to Mars.

Earlier this year, astronauts completed a lunar flyby during the Artemis II mission. Artemis III is scheduled to test spacecraft and landing systems in Earth orbit in 2027, while Artemis IV is expected to attempt a lunar landing in early 2028, before the end of Trump's presidential term.

"Just this week, I issued the American Declaration of Freedom in Space, proclaiming all of space opened for American settlement, American civilization and American freedom," Trump said.

Before introducing the president, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman also discussed the space agency's Mars ambitions and long-term goals.

CHINA IS RACING TO THE MOON, AND AMERICA MUST CLEAR THE PATH FOR SPACE INNOVATION

A "selfie" taken by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover, made up of 62 individual images, on July 23, in this image released Sept. 10, 2025. (NASA handout via Reuters)

He described the administration's ultimate goal as the day "American astronauts plant the Stars and Stripes on Mars."

The administration has previously outlined broader space ambitions, including plans for a U.S. Space Academy, which Trump announced in August. The proposed institution would train students for careers in the Space Force, NASA and the civilian spaceflight industry.

Trump also emphasized his broader vision for American space exploration.

#5998. 'He's got to go': Hakeem Jeffries calls for Hegseth's removal but stops short of impeachment

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., at a news conference in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images hide caption

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat who is poised to become the next Speaker of the House, says his party will push to end the war in Iran and hold Trump administration officials accountable after its midterm victories. But how far Democrats will go remains unclear.

Speaking with Morning Edition on Friday, Jeffries called the conflict a "war of choice" that "has skyrocketed gas prices, diesel prices and fertilizer prices," raising the cost of everyday goods.

He said Democrats "shouldn't have to wait" for the new Congress to act.

But with majorities in both chambers, Jeffries said Democrats could pass a war powers resolution to try and force President Trump to end the war. If passed, it would present President Trump with the choice to either sign or veto it. Overriding a veto would require two-thirds majorities in both chambers. As of now, Democrats are short of a veto-proof majority in both chambers.

Jeffries stopped short of supporting impeachment proceedings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky has threatened to force a House vote on eight articles of impeachment unless Hegseth resigns.

"We'll have that conversation," Jeffries said, calling Hegseth "the most unqualified secretary of defense in American history."

Asked directly whether Hegseth should be impeached, Jeffries said, "I don't want to get out ahead of the caucus."

Jeffries said the House Judiciary and Oversight committees would investigate alleged wrongdoing by the Trump administration.

Asked about voters calling for new Democratic leadership, including the next House speaker, Jeffries said the decision rests with the House Democratic Caucus. He defended Democrats' record, saying they had "battled Trump on every issue up until this point and then just decisively defeated him a few days ago."

Listen to the full interview using the blue button above, or read the transcript below, lightly edited for length and clarity.

Leila Fadel: The person expected to be the next House Speaker and its first Black Speaker is the current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, and he joins me now to talk about what that will look like. So your party has a real mandate here in Congress, and it comes with expectations from voters that you'll make life more affordable. What is at the top of your agenda if you're elected House Speaker?

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries: Well, it was a tremendous victory for the American people and a strong rebuke of MAGA extremism, which has made life more expensive for everyday Americans. Despite their promises to lower the high cost of living on day one. There are several steps that we can take to create a more comfortable way of life for the American people, including ending the war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed gas prices, diesel prices, and fertilizer prices, and as a result, increased the cost of groceries and everyday goods on the American people.

Jeffries: Well, we shouldn't have to wait till the new Congress until that happens. The American people have clearly spoken. Even the Vice President has expressed an understanding that it's time to end the war, or Republicans will continue to pay electoral consequences in that regard, but in the majority, having both the House and the Senate, we can advance strong war powers resolutions that the president will have to take up, get it to his desk, and then explain himself to the American people if, in fact, he decides to use his veto pen.

Fadel: Do you think he'll be willing to work with you on this? I mean, he's given some mixed messages, saying I'm ready to work with the Democrats, but I'll also be "Mr. Veto."

Jeffries: I think it's incredibly important, and that we all listen to what has been expressed by the American people throughout this campaign. We promised that we were going to relentlessly fight for a more affordable America, work to drive down the high price of groceries and gas and housing, fight to make health care affordable for every single American, and at the same period of time hold the crooks accountable for all of the corruption that has been visited upon the American people. And there's an economic cost to corruption that clearly the American people have concluded Republicans have visited upon them. So hopefully, all of my colleagues on the other side of the aisle, as a result of the roaring voices of the American people, will conclude that we should decisively act to make the lives of the American people affordable.

Fadel: I want to ask about a pressing matter. Republican Congressman and Trump critic Thomas Massie of Kentucky says he'll force a vote on the House floor of eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth if he does not resign. Here's what Hegseth said in response in a video posted online:

"You see, their policies don't work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It's all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me".

Will you and other Democrats vote to impeach if this happens?

Jeffries: We'll have that conversation. We'll have that conversation when we gather as a caucus immediately upon our return, but I've been very clear about my position with respect to Pete Hegseth. He's the most unqualified Secretary of Defense in American history. He should never have been confirmed by Senate Republicans, and we've seen all the damage that he's visited upon the American people, the world, and the Pentagon in terms of military readiness, and so I first called for Pete Hegseth to be fired by Donald Trump in the spring of 2025. I have not changed my position, and he should have resigned or been fired a long time ago. But certainly in the immediate aftermath of the stunning rebuke of MAGA extremism that the American people visited at the polls a few days ago,

Fadel: But is this the way? Should he be impeached?

Jeffries: Well, as I indicated, we'll have that conversation as a caucus together, and I don't want to get out ahead of the caucus, but I've been very strong and clear in my opinions as it relates to Pete Hegseth. He's got to go.

Fadel: You said yesterday that Americans don't want Democrats to get even; they want you to get things done on their behalf, specifically around affordability. Now, Congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming Oversight Committee Chair, struck a very different tone. He posted online, "Lawyer up," and laid out a plan that included investigating the Trump family for possible crimes in the next Congress. Are you on the same page when it comes to accountability?

Jeffries: Yeah. Well, we've repeatedly made clear over the last two years is that we've got to relentlessly make life more affordable for the American people, while at the same period of time, visit accountability on those who have been engaged in law breaking, norm breaking, and unleashing unprecedented corruption on the American people. And so, it's my expectation, and we're working closely, of course, with Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee and Democrats on the Oversight Committee, who will lead our accountability efforts, along with all of the relevant committees across the Congress, because the levels of corruption have been unprecedented, and we've made clear to the American people that if you have folks out there who have been stealing from the American people, shortchanging the American people, or screwing over the American people, we're going to hold the crooks accountable. We're going to function like a separate and co-equal branch of government, as opposed to, unfortunately, what my Republican colleagues have done is to bury their heads in the sand and be nothing more than a reckless rubber stamp for Donald Trump's extreme agenda. So we got to follow the facts. We got to apply the law. We got to be guided by the Constitution, and we have to deliver a government of the people, by the people, and for the people.

Fadel: Now, your party had a historic win this week, but we were out across the country speaking to people, and at the same time as choosing your candidates, voters were expressing dissatisfaction with the party leadership, and what they saw as an inability to stand up to Trump meaningfully. In the last two years, they wanted new blood in the party. They said they want completely new leadership of the party. That includes for a future speaker of the House. What do you say to the voters who are skeptical of Democratic establishment leaders like yourself?

Jeffries: Well, we're going to put it into the hands of the House Democratic Caucus as we chart a path forward. But we've battled Trump on every issue up until this point, and then just decisively defeated him a few days ago.

#5989. Health intel-sharing group warns industry in wake of cyberattack on French blood bank

A close up of the hands of a nurse from the French Blood Establishment checking the identification and traceability of blood samples beside a donor during a mobile blood donation session in Paimpol Cotes d Armor Brittany France on July 23, 2026. Helene Rigny/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

In a new security bulletin, the information sharing and analysis center devoted to the healthcare industry, Health ISAC, alerted members to a recent wave of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers — including one incident that affected a major French blood bank.

"This alert is issued for situational awareness, highlighting how recent operational technology (OT) attacks against specific refrigeration brands directly intersect with emerging threats to the health sector," reads the bulletin seen by NPR. Operational technology refers to the machines that control physical processes in the real world, from cooling systems to water pumps.

Cyberattacks on grocery stores and food processing plants everywhere from Europe and Israel to U.S. military bases have drawn headlines in recent months, particularly as attacks have resulted in spoiled food, fires, broken machinery, and major business disruptions. Attackers are clearly aware of the vulnerability of these systems and are taking advantage.

However, until news broke that the French blood bank, known as the French Blood Establishment, had also been targeted, there was less public attention focused on the potential consequences of refrigeration controllers failing in other industries, particularly healthcare, where lifesaving implements like blood and vaccines often require finely tuned temperature-controlled environments to remain viable.

"This incident underscores a stark operational reality: cybersecurity in healthcare is fundamentally about patient safety," wrote Errol Weiss, the chief security officer at Health ISAC in an email to NPR. "When threat actors manipulate operational technology like cold-chain storage and refrigeration units holding donor blood, plasma, or critical therapies, they aren't merely stealing data or locking down administrative files, they are directly endangering the physical resources required to sustain human life."

On Thursday, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture published their own fact sheet about threats to industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems, tools they identify as critical to multiple industries from healthcare to chemical production, food and agriculture, and transportation.

The FBI Cyber Branch Operations director, Brett Leatherman, said the bureau is tracking bad actors targeting these systems "across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk."

"Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," Leatherman said.

The French blood bank confirmed in a press release Tuesday that one of its vendors used in cold storage rooms was targeted by malicious cyber activity, resulting in the defrost and temperature thresholds being raised dangerously high. The French Blood Establishment ultimately managed to detect the suspicious activity in time to rescue blood samples.

It remains unclear who is responsible for the global attacks on refrigeration controllers, and whether it's multiple actors or groups.

Iran has been linked to at least one incident in Israel earlier in the spring, though that breach involved a lot more sophistication and malicious activity. Investigators probing the disruptions at U.S. military bases are also considering Iran as the potential culprit.

Meanwhile, two pro-Russian hacking groups, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance, belatedly released videos and posted on Telegram claiming responsibility for the attacks across Europe, publishing a sample of alleged hacked credentials that would've allowed them to access equipment including machines made by the Danish company Danfoss and the American company Copeland. Those machines can monitor and control temperature and other functions. The hacking groups have some history of targeting refrigeration controllers and other operational technology. However, it's unclear if the recent wave of attacks on refrigerators and freezers across Europe even required stolen credentials to execute, a factor that has led some cybersecurity experts to be skeptical of their claims.

Even so, it will require more evidence like access logs, configuration changes, and connections between maintenance accounts on the controllers to make any clear assessments, explained Tom Hegel, who leads threat intelligence research at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne.

"Russian-aligned actors are a credible hypothesis because there is a credible precedent, including the refrigeration-related attack DOJ attributed to CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn and NoName's history of politically motivated disruption. But that is only the context, not the missing evidentiary link to these European incidents," Hegel told NPR.

"It's important to note that such Russian threat actors often seek attention and claim to cause incidents even when false," he continued.

Regardless of who's responsible, the incident highlights how these nearly ubiquitous tools used to remotely manage critical systems are vulnerable to attack in several different ways.

For one, thousands of the refrigeration controllers in France alone were exposed to the open internet with almost no protection put in place before unidentified hackers went after them in October. Afterward, experts were still tracking hundreds of devices left unprotected. That's just a fraction of the tens of thousands of exposed operational devices online, many of them embedded in critical infrastructure.

Additionally, many of the major remote management systems used in refrigerators and freezers have security vulnerabilities. After alerting the companies to the problems, cybersecurity firm Claroty published research on vulnerabilities in multiple major refrigeration controllers, including those made by both the American manufacturer Copeland and by Danfoss.

While some of those vulnerabilities have been discovered and the vendors have designed patches to seal the hole, the problems don't stop there.

Experts warn it's difficult to patch operational technology because doing so often requires shutting systems down. In industries like healthcare, even minutes of downtime create extreme risk for patient safety. And for some aging models, it's impossible to patch, because the vendor is no longer offering updates — and companies can't afford to spring for a new model.

Sometimes, executives don't even know what machines are on their networks.

Additionally, for many companies, vendors that work with them demand remote access to systems like refrigeration controllers to regularly service them. It's often a requirement in the contract companies sign.

"Industrial chillers operate under vendor contracts that mandate persistent remote access," explained Nic Adams, CEO of 0rcus, a U.S. offensive security firm. "These commercial agreements leave national food and medical supplies defenseless against basic credential abuse."

Finally, hackers are now using AI to find these vulnerabilities faster than ever, and AI is also helping them to better understand the complex machines and the processes they control. Bad actors a world away no longer need to understand individual languages or industries, or even the physics involved to disrupt operations. In recent weeks, cyber incident responders tell NPR they're seeing a massive spike in attacks that are at least in part carried out by AI agents.

The good news is that a lot of these attacks, even if they incorporate AI, are not particularly sophisticated, novel, or stealthy.

Weiss of Health ISAC tells NPR there are basic steps the healthcare industry can take to prevent being a victim of these opportunistic attacks.

That process "begins" by "eliminating public internet exposure," wrote Weiss, then "enforcing strict network segmentation" in order to isolate refrigeration systems "from standard enterprise and guest networks" and finally adding on safeguards "that software overrides cannot bypass" like "hard-wired mechanical cutoffs" and "independent thermal alarms."

In the Health ISAC alert, the industry is urged to separate not just refrigeration controllers from hospital IT systems, but also medical gas monitors, for one, and train staff onsite on how to take physical manual control of machines in an emergency.

Finally, the alert urges hospitals to have offline backups of their systems.

Sharing intelligence about these kinds of cyberattacks can help other potential victims avoid disaster.

While Estonian grocery stores were targeted in the most recent wave of attacks, many of those store managers were on high alert thanks to warnings issued by Estonia's Information Systems Authority, RIA. "When one Selver store was attacked on 2 November, the attackers managed to change the refrigeration system's temperature setting to +50°C. However, the service provider reacted quickly and prevented significant damage," said Annika Müür, a spokesperson for RIA. "So while we can't say that Estonia managed to prevent the attacks entirely, I think this case is a good example of the importance of monitoring threats internationally, acting on early warnings and working closely with businesses to minimise the impact."

Weiss of Health ISAC also urged companies across sectors that are being targeted by this recent wave of attacks to share information to help others defend themselves.

"The attack highlights why timely, trusted information sharing across borders and sectors is our strongest collective defense," he wrote.

"Rapid intelligence sharing allows hospitals and health facilities globally to recognize emerging attack patterns, verify vendor exposure, and harden critical infrastructure before threat actors can cause physical harm."

#5987. Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as Trump's chief of staff

White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles (R) waves while walking to board Air Force One with White House communications aide Danielle Alvarez (L) and White House Deputy Chief of Staff and Homeland Security Advisor Stephen Miller on October 23, 2026 at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. Alex Wong/Getty Images hide caption

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles is being replaced by Stephen Miller, President Trump said Friday.

The change comes after Republicans were swept out of power during this week's midterm elections and marks a defiant note from Trump. Miller has been the architect of many of Trump's most controversial policies, dating back to his first term, particularly on immigration. Data show voters this week supported Democrats in part because of Trump's aggressive immigration enforcement.

"Stephen's been with me since the beginning. He gets it," Trump told reporters later in the afternoon.

The president said in a post on his platform Truth Social that Wiles - who was the nation's first female White House chief of staff - would continue to work for him on political operations.

"I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First," Wiles said in a statement on X, the social media site. "While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will."

Miller currently serves as deputy chief of staff in the White House, as well as an advisor to the Department of Homeland Security, and will take over on Monday.

Wiles worked with the Trump 2020 campaign in Florida and has served as chief of staff in this White House from day one. She built a reputation as a strict manager who has reduced the staff turnover and volatility of press leaks which plagued Trump's first term in the White House.

Wiles has not given many media interviews herself, but said in a profile for Vanity Fair magazine last year, that Trump "has an alcoholic's personality," but that she was accustomed to dealing with such temperaments. "I make a speciality of it," she told the journalist Chris Whipple.

She was diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year, but it was announced she was cancer free this fall.

Miller has been a fixture in Trump's circles since 2016 with a focus on immigration but has also been involved advising military operations in the Middle East.

In his new role, he is likely to exercise even greater influence over the president's time and attention.

The speechwriter and advisor is known for his rhetorical pugnacity and frequently appears behind Trump in the Oval Office during media events.

Miller has been unapologetic for some of the administration's most controversial actions, particularly aggressive anti-immigration crackdowns that have been popular with Trump's core voting base.

Democratic leaders on Capitol Hill disparaged the move.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries - widely expected to become the new House speaker - said: "Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands. His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today."

And Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer added: "Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat. Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn't have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way."

The chief of staff is a "very important gatekeeper of the president's time, and of their information and the people that are going in to see the president," said David Cohen, a political science professor at the University of Akron who studies the role of the chief of staff.

"One of the things that they're supposed to do is kind of be a neutral broker to make sure all the voices get heard. Oftentimes, though, the chief of staff is the last person talking to the president," said Cohen.

#5985. No one knows how many ballots are outstanding in Mississippi's Senate race

Two Madison County election commissioners inspect an affidavit ballot envelope on Thursday in Canton, Miss. The state's razor-thin U.S. Senate race is shining a spotlight on Mississippi's election processes. Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images hide caption

In Mississippi's too-close-to-call U.S. Senate race, every ballot matters.

But no one can say for sure how many ballots there are left to count.

The razor-thin margin between incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom is shining a light on an election process in Mississippi that is among the slowest and most decentralized in the country. It also doesn't have any provisions for recounts.

"Mississippi is not a model of election administration," said Michael Morse, a law professor at the University of Pennsylvania who studies voting.

As of mid-afternoon Friday, more than 2,000 votes separated the two Senate candidates. But information about exactly how many ballots were outstanding was hard to come by.

The Colom campaign said late Tuesday it was aware of more than 15,000 provisional ballots, which require verification before they're counted. And the chair of the state Republican Party said Thursday he thought there were 20,000 outstanding ballots, including potential absentee votes that can legally be received by officials until Nov. 10 if they were postmarked by Election Day.

Mississippi's top voting official, Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson, said counties run their own elections, and even his office didn't know how many provisionals were left to count. He said midday Friday over 9,000 of them had been processed.

"Until we have the certified results, the individual counties will be the best source of the latest and most up-to-date information," Watson said in a statement. There are 82 counties in Mississippi, and they are not required to transmit election results to the state until next week.

Morse said he was shocked by the lack of good information available for such a high-profile race.

"Right now I would love to know a lot of things about the process and I am struggling to figure out what is unfolding here," Morse said. "I cannot tell you basic things."

What is becoming clear is that the rate of provisional ballots, which are called affidavit ballots in Mississippi, may end up being among the highest in the country this election cycle. Those ballots are cast by people whose eligibility is questionable, according to local officials, so those votes are segregated and officials decide on a case-by-case basis whether they will be counted.

If the Colom campaign's estimate of 15,000 affidavit ballots holds true, that would represent roughly 1.5% of the total ballots cast in the Senate race, according to unofficial results.

In the last midterm year, 2022, just four states had a provisional ballot rate higher than that, according to federal data. And Mississippi looks to have a provisional rate close to double of that in North Carolina this year, based on the preliminary data in both states.

One potential reason is an in-the-weeds detail on how Mississippi does voter registration.

In most states, when voters don't cast ballots over a certain number of election cycles, or local officials come across data that indicates a voter has moved or is ineligible for some other reason, they move that voter to what's known as "inactive" status. But the voter is still able to vote normally for a period of a few years, mandated by federal law, before they either confirm their eligibility or are eventually removed.

Mississippi is one of the few states that makes those "inactive" voters have to vote provisionally. That means those voters need to fill out another form and their information needs to be reviewed after the fact by local officials before their votes are counted.

It's unclear at this point why so many voters had questionable eligibility when they showed up to vote, although the local outlet Mississippi Today has reported extensively on the state's experimental use of credit data to cull voter lists.

Morse said that list maintenance technique is garnering attention, but it's not the whole story.

"It's pairing the experiment with credit data, which could introduce some unreliability, with an undermining of the typical procedural process [in many other states], where a voter [marked "inactive"] could cast a regular ballot for at least the next two federal general elections," Morse said.

Watson, the Republican secretary of state, has already come out in defense of the state's registration process.

"The extra few minutes it may take to vote via affidavit ballot are well worth the election integrity added by having cleaner voter rolls!" Watson wrote Tuesday in a post on X.

But Kathy Boockvar, the former Democratic secretary of state of Pennsylvania, told NPR that while many people who have to vote with a provisional ballot are likely to be ultimately deemed eligible, the process doesn't breed trust from those who have to interact with it.

"It feels like you have to go talk to the teacher or something in the back room," Boockvar said. "It's a little bit of a suspicious-seeming thing because somebody who's going through it generally thinks that they're eligible to vote and feels like they're being asked to do something other than that."

Boockvar added that the fact that information has been so hard to come by is a sign Mississippi hasn't been in the limelight like traditional battleground states before.

"We all have to be prepared whether we expect it or not," Boockvar said. "Transparency and good data is one of the best solutions we have to combating all the suspicion and distrust."

#5980. The incoming class of U.S. senators is full of historic firsts

Josh Turek, Peggy Flanagan, and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed are among several Democratic Senators-elect who made history on Election Day 2026. Scott Olson/Getty Images; Dymanh Chhoun/Sahan Journal/CatchLight via Getty Images; Sylvia Jarrus for NPR hide caption

When the newest class of U.S. senators are sworn into office in January, it will include some of America's firsts.

The 2026 midterm election resulted in a significant shift in the landscape of Congress as Democrats won in a big way up and down the ballot. While not all the races have been called, Democrats have flipped more than 40 House seats and picked up 7 Senate seats, giving them control of both chambers of Congress.

Here are some of the new faces to expect in the Senate who made history on Election Day.

Josh Turek speaks during an election night event Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. Ellen Schmidt/AP hide caption

Turek will be the first Paralympian to serve in the Senate. The Democrat is a two-time gold medalist in wheelchair basketball. Turek is paraplegic and uses a wheelchair due to spina bifida. He beat Republican Ashley Hinson in the general election.

Julia Letlow speaks to media during an election night watch party on May 16, 2026, in Baton Rouge, La. Matthew Hinton/AP hide caption

Letlow has now made history twice. She was the first Republican woman elected to the U.S. House from Louisiana in 2021. Letlow ran for the House in a special election to replace her late husband, Congressman Luke Letlow, who died of COVID-19 in 2020. Now, Louisiana voters have decided to send her to the Senate, where she will be the first Republican woman from the state to serve. She will succeed Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, who Letlow beat in the primary election.

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed visits a polling precinct on the campus of the University of Michigan on November 3, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Mich. Salwan Georges/Getty Images hide caption

The incoming Democratic senator is the son of Egyptian immigrants and is the first Muslim person elected to the upper chamber. El-Sayed is an epidemiologist and the former health director for the city of Detroit. He beat Republican Mike Rogers for the hotly contested seat.

Peggy Flanagan walks with her husband as they arrive to vote at a polling location on Election Day in St. Louis Park, Minn. on November 3, 2026. Tim Evans/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Minnesota's Democratic Lt. Governor is the first Native American woman elected to the Senate. Flanagan is a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe. She also made political history more than once. She was also the first woman of color elected to state office in Minnesota. Flanagan will replace outgoing Democratic Sen. Tina Smith.

Chris Pappas walks onstage to deliver his acceptance speech at a watch party at the Puritan Backroom on November 3, 2026 in Manchester, New Hampshire. Joseph Prezioso/Getty Images hide caption

Pappas is the first openly gay man elected to the Senate and is also the first gay man to represent the state of New Hampshire. He served four terms in the House and beat Republican John Sununu in the election.

Dr. Annie Andrews takes the stage at an election night event in Charleston, S.C. on November 3, 2026. Mic Smith/AP hide caption

In one of the biggest election night upsets, Andrews pulled out an underdog win in deep red South Carolina. Andrews is the first woman elected to the U.S. senate from the Palmetto State. She beat Darline Graham, who was appointed to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham.

Democratic candidates James Talarico and Adam Hamilton won their Senate races in Texas and Kansas, respectively. Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images; Charlie Riedel/AP hide caption

Both states are reliably Republican and both states are sending pastors to Washington. This midterm election voters broke with the status quo and elected Democrats to represent them in the Senate.

In Texas, voters selected Democrat James Talarico as their next senator. It is the first time the Longhorn State has sent a Democrat to the chamber since 1988. Talarico won against Republican nominee Ken Paxton.

After nearly 100 years, Kansas elected a democratic senator to the chamber. Adam Hamilton will be the first Democrat that has served the state since 1932. He fended off a tough race with incumbent Republican Roger Marshall.

A previous version of this story incorrectly said Peggy Flanagan is the first Native American elected to the U.S. Senate. She is the first Native American woman elected to the upper chamber.

#5951. PJM’s Emergency Order Should Be a Wake-Up Call for Michigan: Build More Power Before the Next Crisis

By Terence Parker, Michigan resident and Solar Mounts LLC team member

The U.S. Department of Energy’s October 12, 2026, emergency order directing PJM Interconnection to use additional generating resources should be a wake-up call for Michigan and the entire PJM region. Effective October 13–16, the order authorizes specified power plants to operate as needed for reliability and allows backup generators at large facilities to help reduce grid demand during emergencies.

This does not mean blackouts are inevitable. However, it highlights the serious challenges facing our electricity system and the need to add capacity before emergency measures become routine.

As a Michigan-based company, Solar Mounts LLC, a designer and manufacturer of commercial and utility-scale solar mounting systems, recognizes the potential implications for electricity prices, air quality, local businesses, and families across the state.

Rising Costs and the Consequences of Delayed Generation

PJM’s capacity auctions have exposed the difficulty of securing enough electricity for future demand. Prices reached $329.17 per megawatt-day for the 2026–2027 delivery year and $333.44 for 2027–2028, with the latter auction falling short of PJM’s stated reliability requirement.

Source: Vicinity Energy’s Analysis of PJM Capacity Auctions

Capacity costs are only one component of electricity bills, but rising prices signal growing pressure on consumers. We need more power before shortages force increasingly expensive emergency responses.

The October 2026 order permits designated generating units to exceed specified operating limits when necessary for reliability. It also authorizes PJM to direct backup generation at data centers and other large facilities, potentially including diesel generators as a last resort.

Running fossil-fuel plants more frequently can increase emissions, depending on the units involved. Operating diesel generators will worsen local noise pollution and expose operators to high diesel prices. If these measures become more common, we should ask why cleaner generation and storage are not coming online faster.

Weather Uncertainty Makes Planning Urgent

NOAA’s October 15, 2026, winter outlook anticipates warmer-than-average conditions across much of the northern United States, including the Midwest, influenced by a strong El Niño.

Source: NOAA’s 2026–2027 U.S. Winter Outlook

Seasonal forecasts cannot predict every period of extreme demand. Aging infrastructure, maintenance, changing weather, and growing electricity consumption reinforce the need for advance planning. Temporary authority to run additional fossil-fuel resources cannot replace long-term investment in generation.

Solar, Wind, and Batteries Can Help Close the Gap

Utility-scale solar, wind, and battery storage can help meet demand on timelines that many conventional generation projects cannot match. Suitable solar projects may be built within 18 months, depending on permitting, equipment, and interconnection. New nuclear facilities generally require substantially longer development periods.

Solar and wind will reduce emissions when they displace electricity from fossil-fuel generators. Batteries store surplus electricity for periods of higher demand. Note: actual emissions benefits depend on which generators are displaced and when electricity is delivered.

Faster interconnection reviews are also essential. Qualified solar projects shouldn’t remain in queues for years because of avoidable administrative delays. Better coordination among PJM, utilities, regulators, developers, and state governments, alongside necessary transmission upgrades, will bring capacity online sooner.

Solar Development and Agriculture Can Coexist

At Solar Mounts LLC, we witness concerns about installing solar on productive farmland here in rural Calhoun County (home to Solar Mounts LLC). However, well-designed projects can include restoration plans that allow agricultural use to resume when leases end. Solar leases can also provide farmers with supplemental income when crop prices fail to keep pace with production costs.

Agrivoltaic systems combine electricity generation with compatible crops or livestock. Thoughtful design and community engagement can balance renewable energy development with agricultural productivity, rural traditions, and farmland preservation.

Opportunities extend beyond prime farmland. Parking lots, commercial properties, brownfields, landfills, and other underutilized sites can accommodate solar generation. Solar carports provide electricity, shade, and weather protection, while community solar expands access for people unable or unwilling to install their own panels.

Solar Mounts LLC supports practical, site-appropriate solutions that expand generation while respecting farmers, landowners, and rural communities.

Hyperscale Data Centers Must Help Provide Their Own Power

Growing data center demand, particularly in Virginia and other parts of PJM’s territory, is adding pressure to an already constrained grid. Consequently, developers of new hyperscale facilities should demonstrate how they will secure adequate electricity and pay their fair share of supporting infrastructure. Dedicated generation, renewable energy contracts, batteries, flexible demand, and grid upgrades can all contribute.

Requiring every facility to build a gas-fired peaker plant is not necessarily the best answer. Gas turbines face equipment and supply-chain constraints, while additional fossil-fuel generation carries emissions and operating costs. A combination of solutions tailored to each location is more practical.

Existing facilities should also reduce peak demand where possible. Energy efficiency remains one of the most immediate ways businesses can limit electricity consumption.

Solar Mounts LLC sees the opportunity to expand commercial and utility-scale solar infrastructure across Michigan and the country. We encourage this expansion by supporting faster approvals, better grid planning, and a serious commitment to adding power generation and energy storage before shortages worsen.

Reliable electricity underpins our economy, jobs, and daily lives. Repeated emergency orders, rising capacity costs, and greater reliance on high-emission generation are not sound long-term strategies.

We shouldn’t wait for the next crisis to build the power system we already know we need.

#5947. Donated solar project powers community center in unincorporated New Mexico village  Solar Power World’s Projects of Impact

A building that started as a one-room schoolhouse has through the decades expanded to become a lifeline for a New Mexico community far from any city infrastructure, and a recent solar installation has brought new resilience to this place.

Children run outside of Ojo Sarco, New Mexico’s one-room schoolhouse in a photo from January 1943. The structure still stands today as the Ojo Sarco Community Center. Credit: John Collier, Jr./Library of Congress

The structure housing the Ojo Sarco Community Center (OSCC) was founded in the early 20th century. Ojo Sarco is an unincorporated community home to about 300 people that is located about 43 miles northeast from Santa Fe.

“We have no political voice, really,” said Carol Miller, a grant writer and board member for the Ojo Sarco Community Center. “We’re pretty neglected. We’ve lost resources in the past. We were the first wave of people to lose our post office many years ago. Everybody has to commute pretty much for everything.”

That commute is about 40 minutes round trip for basic amenities, she said.

The community center has tried to fill in those resource gaps with services like a twice-monthly food bank, summer meal programs for kids, safety classes and outings for its residents, such as a night at the opera. The OSCC also recently met all the qualifications to be a state library.

PPC Solar, also known as Paradise Power Company, from Taos, built a 7.5-kW solar project paired with 10.6-kWh of LFP energy storage at the OSCC. The contractor built the array at no-cost to the community center. Every year PPC donates a solar array to a regional nonprofit organization, and after three years of applying, the OSCC was awarded the project.

CEO Daniel Weinman’s father founded Paradise Power Company in the 1970s, and the company has installed solar in off-the-grid communities since the start. Its PV donation program is built out of that tradition.

“We’ve always wanted to find a way to give back to the community,” Weinman said. “The best thing that we found — and we’ve been doing it for over a decade now — is doing an annual nonprofit donation system … We’ve had farming organizations, land conservation organizations, and it goes on and on. Really, it’s about finding the right fit. We wanted to make a good impact for this community center, and we felt resiliency was the best way to do that.”

Solar Power World spoke to both PPC Solar and organizers with the OSCC about what effect this solar project has had in the village since it was built in fall 2025.

Larry Miller, project manager and OSCC board member: I think it’s a transformative project for our small community. We like to talk about the history of the community center, and now this is part of it. If someone doesn’t notice the solar panels on the roof, we point it out to them. It’s integrated into our lives here.

Carol Miller: It’s lowered our electric costs, which is really important for us, because we’re such a shoe-string operation. We’ve had some fun talks with the community because they all know we’ll have the charging capacity. We still have internet available, even with the power out. All the kids that come to our library programs, they’re solar oriented. The benefit of this company and its staff just has ripple effects throughout our greater community.

PPC Solar donated a solar plus storage project to the Ojo Sarco Community Center. This array will keep power running in this facility that has become a haven for Ojo Sarco residents. Credit: PPC Solar

Preston Bastardo, sales and design, PPC Solar: The building itself had some challenges with mounting the array on the roof, but that just took some exploration in the attic and making sure that we could land things where we needed to. The building has two large areas, and so fo installation of batteries had some restrictions, there was a good mechanical closet that we were able to use for batteries. Then as far as backup circuits, we did a partial facility backup where we had a critical loads panel next to their main panel. I think everything went pretty smoothly.

Weinman: Well, it really goes back to our roots. In 1972, there was no technology supporting solar at the time. My dad was a pioneer in the industry and he really developed his own controls and safety protections and found used panels and used batteries and was bringing power to places where there was no power. Our house, for example, we started with kerosene lanterns. We didn’t have electricity until we had a solar power system, and it was really life changing.

Being able to build on that legacy and look at our community in that light and be able to offer systems like this to communities that need it — I think that really adds to that legacy and really is profound in a lot of ways. It feels great to be able to do this and be in a position where we can help others realize and experience the benefits of solar power. We want to continue to participate in any way we can.

Carol Miller: We’re a very old community and proud of it. And having worked with local businesses and our electrical co-op, we know it’s really the exception and not the rule because we own our power. Any technology that is shared equally in a low-income community has ripple effects beyond what I think some of us imagined a number of years ago. It’s for everyone.

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5941. APS expects sales to double by 2041, plans extending coal use to 2038

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Peak demand will grow about 3.4% annually over the next 15 years, driven by industry and data centers, Arizona Public Service said in an integrated resource plan filed Friday with regulators.

APS projects peak demand of more than 14.5 GW in 2041, almost 60% higher than its current record peak of about 9.2 GW, set in August. And the utility expects annual retail sales to grow to about 80,600 GWh in 2041, up from about 34,200 GWh in 2025.

There is some uncertainty behind APS’ load projections, but the utility said it has taken steps to protect customers.

Despite refinements to APS’ large-load interconnection process, the “sustained record levels of interest” from large customers poses “a risk in increased potential for unrealized loads,” APS said in its resource plan, which it files every three years with the Arizona Corporation Commission. To mitigate the risk, APS said it adopted strategies such as having customers commit to “minimum demand and energy-based contract terms, providing collateral in case of default, and instituting early exit fees.”

As a result of population growth and higher levels of economic activity, APS said it expects to add up to 29,000 residential customers annually in the near term, and across the planning period the utility anticipates annual customer growth to be in the range of 1.5% to 2.5% through 2030.

The utility’s preferred plan includes continuing to operate the Four Corners coal plant beyond a planned 2031 retirement. APS said the extension could save customers close to $1 billion.

“The company will continue to evaluate the appropriate time to cease operations between 2031 and 2038, with the decision depending on customer needs, economics and other factors evaluated through future planning processes,” APS said in a statement.

“Reliability is nonnegotiable,” Mike Eugenis, APS director of resource planning, said in a statement.

APS’ planned natural gas resource additions include repowering the Cholla Power Plant as a 387-MW facility by 2030, adding 1,107 MW through new combustion turbines at existing APS sites and uprates to tolling units during 2026-2030, according to the IRP. Under the plan, APS will also add the 1,238 MW Desert Sun combined-cycle facility in 2032 to serve large-customer subscription load.

Customer and clean energy advocates were critical of the APS plan.

APS’ proposal “further delays our move from gas and coal to solar and wind,” Sierra Club Grand Canyon Chapter Director Sandy Bahr said in a statement. “We’re seeing these utilities protect their own bottom lines, instead of making the most economical decisions for ratepayers.”

The utility “should be investing in proven community-based energy solutions, like local solar and battery storage,” Vote Solar West Senior Regulatory Director Kate Bowman said in a statement.

APS “failed to consider how alternative technologies like rooftop solar, battery storage, and other distributed resources could help meet energy needs,” Bowman said. As the ACC considers the plan, regulators will have “an opportunity to push for a more comprehensive approach that puts affordability, reliability, and the interests of customers at the center of long-term planning,” she added.

The utility said it is adding nearly 2 GW of renewable utility-scale solar and 2.5 GW of battery storage in the next two years, “diversifying our resources to keep energy reliable and affordable.” By 2030, APS said it expects to have approximately 6 GW of battery storage on its system.

The utility also expects continued growth in customer-sited resources. APS said behind-the-meter storage adoption is expected to grow every year to 1.2 GW by 2045 — up from 69 MW today. For 2032, the storage forecast is approximately 95% higher compared to the last storage forecast developed in 2023, APS said.

Behind-the-meter solar adoption is expected to slow relative to the 2020-2023 period but “will still experience some modest growth,” reaching 3.7 GW by 2045 — up from 2.1 GW today.

Electric vehicles in APS service territory are expected to grow from 65,000 vehicles today to 1.1 million in 2045, resulting in 5.2 TWh of EV charging load, APS said. In 2042, this forecast is approximately 18% lower compared to the last EV forecast developed in 2023, it noted.

#5935. Exelon, Invenergy complaints at FERC seek capacity market changes

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Exelon asked the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to order PJM to adopt a “prompt” capacity auction; Invenergy wants the Midcontinent grid operator to let HVDC lines receive capacity payments.

Exelon and Invenergy Transmission this week filed separate complaints at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission seeking changes to the capacity markets run by the PJM Interconnection and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator.

Exelon asked FERC to order PJM to shift to a “prompt” auction from its current forward capacity auction schedule, according to a Tuesday filing at the agency. Currently, PJM holds annual base capacity auctions to secure power supplies three years in advance.

Under Exelon's proposal, PJM would hold its capacity auctions two months before the delivery year begins, starting with the 2030/31 delivery year. If FERC approves the proposal, PJM would hold its next capacity auction in December for the 2029/30 delivery year as planned, and then it would hold its next auction in early 2030.

Pushing out the date of the 2030/31 auction would give PJM time to overhaul its capacity market, which Exelon contends is no longer working properly, according to the complaint.

Adopting a prompt auction would help ensure that auctions are based on more accurate load forecasts, resource availability data and capacity accreditation levels, Exelon said. It would also facilitate more efficient resource entry and exit through improved market signals, the Chicago-based utility company said. Exelon’s utilities have about 10.7 million customers in PJM’s Mid-Atlantic and Midwest footprint.

Exelon asked FERC to make a decision on the complaint by Jan. 31, the last day before PJM is set to release the planning parameters for the 2030/31 delivery year base auction, which is set to be held in May.

PJM is reviewing the complaint and will reply at “the appropriate time,” Jeffrey Shields, a PJM spokesman, said.

The grid operator is accepting proposals from stakeholders on how it could reform its capacity market through its Power Reliability Through Market Design initiative, Shields noted. PJM has received more than 30 responses to its request for papers on the issue. They will be discussed at a Nov. 13 workshop.

When it kicked off the effort in May, PJM proposed three broad reform pathways: stabilizing its existing capacity market, rationing grid reliability among customer classes or regions and shifting to a market focused on energy and ancillary services and away from the capacity market.

Meanwhile, Invenergy Transmission on Wednesday told FERC that MISO improperly bars high-voltage, direct-current merchant transmission lines from its capacity market.

MISO counts the capacity value of HVDC lines when it decides how much capacity it needs to buy in its capacity auctions, a move that reduces the amount of capacity it acquires, according to the complaint.

But, MISO’s rules prevent those lines from being accredited as capacity resources or their owners otherwise being paid for their capacity value, allowing the grid operator to benefit from the lines for free, Invenergy said.

“MISO cannot rely on that capacity, to the benefit of other customers, while refusing to provide any avenue for the entity that provides that capacity to receive commensurate compensation,” the Chicago-based company said.

Instead of recovering their costs through FERC-approved cost-of-service rates, the owners of merchant lines recover their costs via rates negotiated with their customers, Invenergy noted.

“Interregional merchant HVDC transmission lines only receive compensation if there is a product or service — such as capacity — for which they can transact with potential customers,” Invenergy said.

Without capacity payments from MISO, “there is no product or service that can be the basis of a merchant-based transaction in MISO,” Invenergy said.

Using a “direct loss of load” accreditation methodology, Invenergy’s Grain Belt Express HVDC transmission line could provide more than 1,800 MW of accredited capacity, according to the complaint.

The 5-GW, 600-kV Grain Belt project is slated to run about 800 miles from Kansas to Indiana. Invenergy plans to build the roughly $11 billion project in two phases, with the first phase running from southwest Kansas to central Missouri.

#5932. The industry races into Las Vegas for RE+

The largest tradeshow focused on the U.S. solar, storage and clean energy markets is back in Las Vegas for 2026. RE+ was the 24th largest tradeshow in the United States in 2025 by attendance, and this year’s showing (Nov. 16-19) is expected to be just as large.

The Formula 1 series will race the Las Vegas Grand Prix the weekend after RE+ concludes. Photos courtesy: F1 and the Las Vegas Grand Prix

The U.S. solar and storage industries have gotten so big that it appears only the Las Vegas Convention Center can accommodate a tradeshow bringing together nearly 40,000 clean energy professionals in one place. RE+ will be held at the Las Vegas Convention Center each November for the foreseeable future.

The convention center is tucked away from the main strip of casinos, but there is still plenty in the area to see and do. The site is also easily accessible, with a stop on the Las Vegas Monorail.

Conference education programming begins on Monday and sessions continue throughout the show at various stages on the exhibit hall floor. The exhibition opens on Tuesday.

Exhibitors will be spread across three halls in the convention center — the main entrance is at West Hall which extends via an over-street walkway to North Hall, and then Central Hall is accessed beyond a lobby area. There will also be a few outdoor booths to peruse located near food trucks. Visiting outdoor exhibits in November will be more comfortable, as the average high temperature is just 70°F, unlike the late summer heat of September.

Special events at RE+ include a golf tournament on Monday and the Run with the Sun 5K on Tuesday. The “Energy in Motion” block party will be at the Convention Center on Tuesday starting at 7 p.m. in the West Hall.

Formula 1 will race the Las Vegas Grand Prix the weekend following RE+. The course takes drivers down the Las Vegas Strip and around the Sphere, and road closures to the public will begin on Thursday. The Las Vegas Convention Center is several blocks north of the racing circuit, so the conference shouldn’t experience disruptions. After-conference activities might be affected later in the week, and attendees should plan a little extra time getting to the airport if leaving before the weekend.

Solar Power World editors will be covering all the sights at RE+ this year, so be sure to follow along on LinkedIn and right here on the website. But first, here’s a preview of a few must-see booths on the tradeshow floor.

Visit AWM at RE+ to learn about our Strata for BESS cable management solutions. Our Strata Components and Strata System are tailored for leading energy storage applications and engineered for durability and easy installation. Strata supports reliability across the entire lifecycle of stand-alone storage or hybrid renewable power plants.

Construct solar safer, faster, and cheaper. Meet Built’s AI Piling Solution: a fully autonomous piling system for utility-scale solar. Leading contractors are trusting Built to install production-ready piles anywhere, anytime. Head to Central Hall Booth C6310 to learn how to add physical AI to your next solar project.

Hydrelio aiR Optim is our flexible floating racking and anchoring system. It comes from 15+ years of FPV knowledge and expertise, and the first patented and industrialized floating solar solution. It is the result of continuous R&D involvement, innovation, testing and experience building more than 350 FPV arrays worldwide.

IslandDER Meter Socket Adapter (MSA) streamlines solar + storage installs by integrating a microgrid interconnect device (MID), consumption transformers (CTs), voltage sensing and battery communication protocols into a single, compact device that inserts directly into the meter socket in 15 minutes. This eliminates complex electrical work — such as panel upgrades, circuit relocations and gateways — saving installers days of labor on battery backup jobs and preventing unexpected costs for homeowners. Compatible with battery systems from SolarEdge, FranklinWH, Lunar Energy, EcoFlow and Fox ESS, IslandDER is trusted by leading national installers, offering more versatility and compatibility than any meter collar on the market.

Built on gallium nitride (GaN) technology, Enphase’s ninth-generation microinverter platform delivers industry-leading efficiency and cooler operation for residential and commercial systems. IQ9 Microinverters support the latest high-wattage solar panels across single-phase and three-phase applications and seamlessly integrate with IQ Batteries to create a complete AC-coupled solar and storage system.

HD Hyundai Energy Solutions debuts its TOPCon multi-cut module at RE+ 2026, reaching 660 W at 24.4% efficiency. Ultra-precision cutting boosts power density and cell efficiency, backed by the company’s FEOC-compliant, TOPCon-licensed manufacturing capabilities and 20 years of cell-to-module expertise.

Intertek CEA will showcase two new advances in solar quality assurance: AePVI, an aerial inspection service that combines drone and ground-based data with electroluminescence (EL) testing to identify defects across utility-scale projects; and EL-AI, software that reviews the EL image of every module before shipment, moving beyond traditional sample-based inspections.

The OMCO Origin Factory-Direct Trackers and OMCO Choice Fixed-Tilt Mounting Systems support a wide range of solar projects in the utility scale and distributed generation (DG) markets. The OMCO Origin Trackers pair seamlessly with the OMCO Star Tracker Control System that features DC tracker controllers, field-replaceable batteries and a one-mile wireless range for all climates.

The S-5-CP clamp is engineered for mounting solar panels to purlin-framed carport structures. Featuring an optional EPDM gasket for a water-resistant seal, it significantly reduces the risk of leaks while delivering fast, reliable installation. Designed for durable, high-efficiency solar carport applications, it pairs seamlessly with the S-5! PVKIT for rail-less installations.

Built around Siemens’ U.S.-manufactured 375-kW 3TL500 string inverters, WATTBLOC Virtual Central Station (VCS) transforms utility-scale solar through a modular, scalable power-block architecture. Leveraging standardized power-block designs up to 5 MWAC, its distributed architecture improves availability, simplifies maintenance, accelerates deployment, lowers lifecycle costs and supports expansion across utility-scale solar portfolios.

SiteCaptureAI’s contextual AI automates jobsite documentation, quality control and reporting across the full solar project lifecycle, from surveys and installations to O&M and TPO financing. It uses photo and video intelligence to verify field reporting, flag compliance issues and cut QA/QC work, reducing truck rolls and financing rejections.

Sungrow North America will highlight three systems: the PowerTitan 3.0, packing 6.9 MWh into a 20-ft container with a 12,500-cycle life; the PowerStack 255CS, which arrives pre-installed and pre-commissioned; and the SG4400 modular inverter, built from independent power modules that keep a single fault from taking the full unit offline.

As solar matures, installers need new ways to create value beyond installation. At RE+, Tigo will highlight repowering aging systems and adding storage with virtual power plant participation. The booth will feature inverter and battery solutions, repowering resources and VPP capabilities that extend system life and create new revenue opportunities.

Trinasolar and Trina Storage will showcase the highly durable Vertex N Shield PV module, certified to withstand 55-mm direct hail impact and 75-mm impact at a 45° stow angle, the Vertex S+ residential module, with enhanced protections against environmental risk, and the next-gen Elementa + Electra battery energy storage solution (BESS).

Weidmuller’s Weather Stations and String Monitored DC Combiner Boxes deliver comprehensive monitoring for utility-scale solar plants. Weather Stations provide accurate environmental data, cybersecurity, edge processing and flexible sensor integration. String Monitored Combiner Boxes enable real-time string-level performance monitoring, early fault detection, reduced maintenance effort and improved plant ROI and LCOE.

#5929. Trump Wants More Attention For His New Algae Biofuel Showcase

US President Donald Trump has famously transformed the magnificent Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool into a high profile showcase for the algae biofuel industry, and he stands firm in his faith that the tiny green microalgae can produce renewable fuels at scale. In fact, on Monday, November 2, the President held his all-important closing message for the 2026 midterm election cycle right there at the Reflecting Pool. Hey, maybe Trump knows something about algae biofuel…

The Reflecting Pool is a massive body of shallow water that extends from the foot of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, DC. Situated on filled ground in former marshlands, the Reflecting Pool provides a golden opportunity to showcase the ability of the domestic biofuel industry to take advantage of the built infrastructure, rather than taking up valuable farmland with conventional energy crops like corn or soybeans.

Although algae cultivation was probably not the original intention of the Reflecting Pool, it has been a perennial host to algae ever since its construction in the 1920’s, with the humid environment and temperate climate of DC lending a hand.

In earlier years, the Pool was drained and refilled twice a year to control the growth. By the 1990’s, the structure was clearly sinking into the marshes, sparking calls for a major structural overhaul and the addition of a water circulating system.

The soup-to-nuts rehab was completed in 2012, and yet the algae persisted. Finally, when Trump took office for the second time in January of 2025, he lit upon a brilliant idea of turning lemons into lemonade. The Reflecting Pool would be re-made as a monument to the domestic algae biofuel industry.

By the summer of 2026, the transformation was complete and the algae were thriving, as confirmed by satellite imagery. Others mocked, but the President stood by the plan. After all, biomass is a key element in his “American Energy Dominance” policy, and where better to showcase biofuel than in the nation’s capitol, to be seen and admired by millions of tourists.

And so, that explains why Trump chose the Reflecting Pool as the seemingly incongruous scene of his Election Day eve closing message, as reported somewhat incredulously by The Guardian among many others.

“On the eve of a consequential election day, with polls indicating that most voters feel the US president has grown too focused on building projects in the nation’s capital, he stood in front of the newly opened reflecting pool to discuss – in detail – changes to the pool’s pipe, the grass surrounding the area and granite,” observed The Guardian.

Algae biofuel surfaced regularly on the pages of CleanTechnica in the early 2000’s, with the high oil content and rapid growth cycle of algae being the attractions along with the potential for developing next-generation farming and extraction systems leading to a competitive renewable energy resource (see more algae background here).

Not much progress has been made since then, and stakeholders in the field have weathered much skepticism if not downright mockery. A seal of approval from the President of the United States of America is just what the industry needs to get to the next level.

Indeed, a fresh round of activity has surfaced in recent years, with the UK firm HutanBio being one example. The startup aims to generate profitability by leveraging the carbon-capturing angle of algae farming.

Earlier this year Hutan signed an MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) with the Irish firm Utopia World Investment and the biodiesel refiner Wakud International to scale up its algae farming system, with Oman being the location. “Our unique microalgae strain, Sphaerica, is grown in seawater, on non-arable coastal land, using CO₂ and sunlight creating a genuinely low-carbon biocrude stream that the industry currently lacks and urgently needs,” HutanBio says of itself.

As described by HutanBio, Sphaerica yields up to ten times more oil than typical algae biofuel strains. Hutan expects the high level of productivity to dovetail with Oman’s high level of solar radiation, enabling it to leapfrog over its competitors.

The Oman operation is set for operation at a demonstration scale before the end of 2027, which is just around the corner. Meanwhile, Japanese automaker Mazda is also beginning to crack the algae code.

On October 7, Mazda announced that its microalgae biofuel research program has nailed down support from NEDO, the New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization of Japan. The Mazda program is in early stages, with scale-up expected by the 2030’s. If all goes according to plan, Mazda will use its homemade algae biofuel to factory-fill the tanks of every diesel vehicle that rolls off its assembly lines.

Evidently Mazda does not anticipate that drivers can pump out algae biofuel at any corner gas station for their next fill-up. Still, it’s another sign that that years-long research programs are finally leading to commercial application.

For a glimpse into the future, check out newly published research from the Saitama University in Japan. Where conventional systems involve cultivating algae, drying it, and processing it to remove oils, the Saitama team has developed a strain of cyanobacteria (commonly known as blue-green algae) that can express free fatty acids outside of the cell and deposit them directly into a culture medium. Among other benefits, the Saitama system does not require destroying the algae with each harvesting cycle.

As for the US, ExxonMobil was the standard-bearer for early stage algae biofuel research throughout the early 2000’s. By 2017, the company was confident enough to put up millions for an elaborate advertising blitz that showcased its efforts to the world.

Or not, as the case may be. In 2019, Massachusetts State Attorney General Maura Healey filed suit against Exxon, alleging that the biofuel ads were deceptive. “Specifically, the complaint alleges that Exxon systematically and intentionally has misled Massachusetts investors about material climate-driven risks to its business and has deceived consumers about the central role its fossil fuel products play in causing climate change,” AG Healy’s office explained.

Exxon subsequently dropped the program altogether, but the lawsuit persists. Among the details coming to light is a deposition by an Exxon scientist who worked on the algae program. Under questioning by attorneys with the AG’s office, the scientist asserted that the claims in Exxon’s ads were “patently false,” and that he said as much to the company.

It’s too bad Exxon dropped the ball before Trump had a chance to pick up the algae biofuel torch. Oh, well. We’ll always have the Reflecting Pool…

Photo: The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool has been host to thriving populations of algae ever since its construction in the 1920’s (cropped, courtesy of National Parks Service).

#5928. Entergy sees progress on Arkansas data center deal, strong Q3 sales

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The New Orleans-based company separately inked firm pipeline contracts for enough natural gas to support 10 new combined-cycle power plants in Louisiana, CEO Drew Marsh said Monday.

Entergy’s amended application to serve a controversial Google data center will save its Arkansas ratepayers at least $500 million more than the $1.6 billion previously agreed, CEO Drew Marsh told investors Monday during the company’s third-quarter earnings call.

The New Orleans-based utility holding company saw earnings increase more than 20% over the year-ago period helped by warmer-than-average weather across its four-state U.S. territory in the Midcontinent Independent System Operator’s southern zones, he said. Total electricity sales rose 5% year over year.

Entergy made progress on two key regulatory priorities in Louisiana, which accounts for nearly half of the holding company’s retail sales.

State regulators in October approved Entergy Louisiana’s $1.2 billion, 500-kV Babel to Webre transmission project, Marsh said. And Louisiana Public Service Commission staff separately reached a settlement with the utility that Entergy said “resolves all outstanding issues” between the company, LPSC staff and one intervenor in a contested proceeding related to several gigawatts of generation and related infrastructure to serve Meta’s planned Hyperion data center campus.

The LPSC is set to vote on the matter next month, Entergy said.

Meanwhile, Entergy’s Mississippi utility asked state regulators last month for state clearance to issue bonds that would offset approximately $237.8 million of costs related to Winter Storm Fern, which Entergy said caused “severe damage” to its infrastructure.

And in Texas, Entergy said it has energized the Orange County Advanced Power Station, a 1,215-MW combined-cycle gas plant built to support load growth in the state’s southeastern corner.

Entergy filed the amended Google service contract with Arkansas regulators last month. If approved, Entergy would add 350 MW of battery energy storage at two sites and procure 440 MW of solar from Pattern Energy’s nearby Big Island Solar project, the company said in a required securities filing this week.

The Arkansas Public Service Commission is set to hear the matter in January, Entergy said.

The amended contract would expand power demand from Google’s West Memphis data center, but the exact amount and other key details are redacted, the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette reported on Oct 20.

On Monday, Marsh said Google would pay $600 million toward the cost of the battery systems and suggested the tech giant would avoid passing costs to other Entergy ratepayers.

“This agreement ensures that Google will cover its fair share, which includes the cost of the new investments as well as their share of system costs,” Marsh said.

Entergy Arkansas is one of five utility companies owned by Entergy, and earned about 48% of its sales from industrial customers in 2025. The parent company’s four-state territory has been a popular destination for large-scale data centers like Google’s Arkansas project and Meta’s even larger Louisiana campus.

Together, data center and traditional industrial customers account for a large share of Entergy’s expected future sales growth, much of which is not yet reflected in the company’s near-term capital plan, Marsh said.

“We have a strong pipeline of projects in varying stages that are not in our base plan,” he said. “Data center interest remains strong and in the range of 7 [GW] to 12 GW. Our traditional industrial segments continue with discussions for 3 [GW] to 5 GW.”

Those large-load pipeline figures are largely unchanged from recent quarters’ projections. But the company’s projected four-year capital spending has risen significantly over the past year, to about $55 billion as of Sept. 30.

Marsh said the Google contract allows Entergy to keep base rates flat for Arkansas customers. However, that’s not the case in Louisiana, where Meta “is helping [to] offset some [infrastructure] costs, but not necessarily to make it go back to flat like we were in Arkansas,” he said.

To serve the Meta data center, Entergy plans to spend about $12.9 billion to build seven combined-cycle gas-fired power plants with 5,278 MW of combined capacity, plus a $1.4 billion transmission line and 200 MW of battery storage. It has also asked Louisiana regulators to approve a corporate sustainability agreement that would see Meta — doing business as Evest LLC — cover the cost of 2,500 MW of new renewables and energy storage resources.

To support the new gas generation, Entergy inked firm transportation agreements with “large midstream and pipeline companies” for 1.325 billion cubic feet/day of natural gas, Marsh said.

“That's enough for Entergy to supply fuel to 10 new combined cycles in Louisiana … and also helps build new pipeline capacity that benefits our industrial customers' growth,” he said.
