#5840. Thermal Dawn — Thermal Storage Is Cheap Storage

Another great idea from Down Under: Thermal Dawn promises cost effective heating and cooling, mainly by replacing gas boilers in cold climates. CleanTechnica had a chance to interview Nick Zeniou, Founder of Thermal Dawn, recently by phone, fresh after his presentation at Everything Electric. You can hear him explain his revolutionary system here, or here with a little less drama.

Everything Electric was a good opportunity to measure public reaction to the new product. Nick tells me that hundreds of people checked out their stall. “People care about carbon cost and comfort. People don’t compromise on comfort.” Sounds like comfort trumps carbon cost. Homeowners who visited the stand and filled out the survey were focused on sustainability and cost. Nick cautions: “it was an electrification expo crowd, and 50 of the 62 already had solar, so it’s not the whole market.” See the chart below.

Although I live in the warmer part of Australia (Brisbane), many Aussies have to endure cold winters. Nick tells me he is looking at installs in Sydney, Canberra, and Melbourne in the deep south. Thermal Dawn can store heat up to 70 degrees Celsius, or down to 5 degrees. Thermal Dawns’ equipment can run cold or hot water through pipes and radiators that are already installed, depending on the need — without having to run an expensive gas boiler. He describes it as a thermal battery. Just to be clear, it does not generate electricity.

Check out this graph below, which shows the Thermal Dawn system in action at a house in Melbourne during a day in August 2026. It shows room temperature and when the heat pump was running, in 15-minute samples, unedited. The heat pump ran until about 1:45pm, then not again, heated by stored energy through the evening peak.

“What about return on investment,” I asked. He described two systems they have had running over the southern Australian winter which have saved the homeowners approximately AU$1,500 each. “The first was a house in Melbourne, our first install, live since May 2026. The owners charge the system in their retailer’s free three-hour midday window, so the heat for the evening costs them close to nothing. The second was a Warragul (slab-heated home, Victoria): installed in two days in July 2026. Our controls turn the home’s concrete slab into part of the battery, managing when it charges and when it releases heat. On 95% of winter evenings, the heat pumps did not run at all between 5 pm and 9pm. Since commissioning, 70,521 MJ of gas has been avoided by just these two installations.”

Nick further explains: “A standard heat pump draws from the grid during those expensive morning and evening hours. You’ve escaped gas, but you’re still paying premium rates every time the temperature drops at night. Thermal Dawn is different. Our system charges when power is cheapest, a free midday window, your own solar, or late-night off-peak, then delivers that stored warmth through your radiators and underfloor heating all evening, with the compressor off through the expensive hours.

It appears that Thermal Dawn’s secret sauce is “Phase Change Materials.” Naturally, Nick declined to share exactly what Thermal Dawn is using. The system replaces a gas boiler with a combination of reverse cycle heat pump, well insulated water tank, and phase change materials. PCMs are designed to freeze or melt at a specific temperature, storing and releasing heat when they change physical state, usually from solid to liquid. “PCM doubles our heat capacity.” The heating applications I could understand, what about the cooling? “Cool water from the tank runs through a fan coil unit, and the fan blows cool air into the room. Cooling is an optional add-on.” That’s the answer.

How do thermal storage and a home battery/solar system work together? “Thermal storage is cheap storage doing one job very well. Heating, cooling, and hot water are the largest, most predictable loads in the house, and covering them thermally is far cheaper per kWh than covering them from lithium. A battery is expensive storage doing a general-purpose job.

“The practical effect is that your battery stops being the thing that carries your heating. It’s freed up for lights, appliances, the EV, and overnight backup, and it lasts longer for not being cycled hard every winter evening. Homes with a battery already are often the clearest case, because the expensive storage stops being spent on the cheapest possible job.”

Thermal dawn connects to existing hydronic pipework. The gas boiler with its high gas bills is gone. Check out the animation of heat discharge overnight. “The thermal battery charged on solar during the day and now heats the house while the heat pump stays off. It’s an illustration of what the app shows, not a recording of a live home.” For those rooms that don’t have hydronic radiators or underfloor slab heating, Thermal Dawn installs fan coil units. Nick tells me via a followup email that: “It’s a small indoor unit with a water coil and a fan: warm water from the thermal battery runs through the coil, and the fan blows the heating or cooling into the room.”

The heavy technical discussion out of the way, I asked Nick about his background. He grew up in an isolated part of New Zealand. His job was to collect the firewood for the family’s heat source — a fireplace. He had to get the fire going by 4:00 pm or the house would not warm up for the cold evening. Timing was very important, as it is for electricity use.

Nick is a mechanical engineer who has worked across tech companies and startups. While working on installing commercial air conditioning, he came across the idea that became Thermal Dawn. Nick joined the dots between the huge variations in electricity supply cost throughout each 24-hour period, with an average home’s thermal energy needs (up to two-thirds of consumption) and the fact that homes are becoming power stations. Thence to thermal batteries powered by Thermal Dawn technology.

He reminisces about the start of the business: “When our first unit was finished, we loaded it into a ute at 5pm and I drove it down the Hume overnight, Sydney to Melbourne (1000 km), to install it the next morning. We had a four-month-old at home at the time. My wife Linda is my co-founder and leads mechanical design and manufacturing, so while I was on the road, she was looking after a newborn.”

For those who would like to get involved, Nick invites Australian homeowners to sign up here and they’ll be in touch. “Readers overseas: send us a message or request a quote at the same link to register interest. If we hear from enough people in one area, we can bring forward our plans to come there.”

Having proven their point, Thermal Dawn is cleared to sell and installing its first batch now, with a larger product for ducted air conditioning in development. I asked about apartment block heating and Nick confirmed that they are looking at it but want to get the domestic home sorted first.

I asked a couple of followup questions “What about the Victorian government’s position?” Nick’s answer:  “Victoria is set to bring in support for systems like ours from the middle of next year. With the state election in November, there’s talk of a change in direction and of belt-tightening, so we’ve built Thermal Dawn to stand on its own. It saves households money without a subsidy, and any support is a bonus.”

Any plans for installs in Canberra? “Yes. Canberra is one of the best places in Australia for this: cold winters, plenty of hydronic homes, and a territory already moving off gas. We’re talking with installers there now.”

I really appreciate these technological experts when they take the time to explain things to me. Sometimes I feel like Winnie the Pooh — a bear of very little brain. Looks like Thermal Dawn has solved another part of the energy puzzle — good news for homeowners and also for the planet.

David Waterworth is a retired teacher who divides his time between looking after his grandchildren and trying to make sure they have a planet to live on. He is long on Tesla [NASDAQ:TSLA].

#5839. The Tesla Cybertruck Is Dead, And Woke 3 Killed It

The incredible news just keeps coming after Tuesday's huge victory for everyone not named Elon Musk. After a little more than three years blighting our roads, filling divorce court parking lots, and getting recalled for all of its parts falling off, the Tesla Cybertruck is dead. Never trust Elon Musk further than you can throw him, but early Friday morning, Tesla's CEO tweeted that the company will wind down production of the Cybertruck before finally killing it once and for all at some point next year.

Posting at 12:30 a.m. Texas Freedom Time, a very normal time that every major CEO is awake and making important business announcements, Musk tweeted, "Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production." So there's no word twisting or reading between the lines required. Tesla's Texas Gigafactory will cease production of the Cybertruck next year, and that's the only place Tesla builds the Cybertruck.

Yes, you read that right, folks. The Tesla Cybertruck is dead, and Woke 3 killed it. The Jalopnik staff, Barack Obama, and Karl Marx drove to Elon's house and made him do it. We have that power now. There's lightning in our veins, fire in our eyes, and soon to be a path of destruction in our wake. If we can kill the Tesla Cybertruck, what can't we do? Universal healthcare? Abolishing the electoral college? Free trans for everybody? Finally receiving a sincere apology from my mom? In 2027, we're making it happen.

Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production

It's not like it's that crazy for a large, generally established, electric-only automaker to add a pickup truck to its lineup. But it didn't. After the first blush of sales, interest in the truck fell faster than a stock price after a phony product reveal. The problem was, while looks are subjective, Tesla never bothered to make the Cybertruck good. I used hyperbole when I said all the Cybertruck's parts kept falling off. Technically that isn't true. But it's more true than it should be for a vehicle available for sale to the public, driven on public roads. Tesla's May recall over Cybertruck wheels falling off wasn't even the only recall Tesla had to issue over parts falling off the Cybertruck.

The Cybertruck also famously couldn't survive a car wash, got its butt kicked off-road by a Ford F-150, had still more parts flying off on the road, oh yeah, snapped its frame in an off-road test. You know, good, old-fashioned American truck stuff. The fact that, by the time the Cybertruck launched, Musk had made a hard public pivot into Republican politics, spending hundreds of millions of dollars to get Donald Trump elected in exchange for a role gutting regulators, didn't help either. It turns out people who buy electric aren't on Musk's chosen political side.

What's best, from a Republican perspective, is to crush EVs, see them driven before you, and hear the lamentations of the EVs' women. So they aren't what business consultants would call "the most reliable buyers of electric pickup trucks." Throw in prices being far higher after launch than we were originally told, and it shouldn't be surprising that sales were almost as terrible as talking to the owners.

But soon, that will all be over. The Tesla Cybertruck will be no more, and Woke will have won. What a wonderful way to wrap up this already incredible election season. Republicans lost, Elon lost, Texas went blue, the Cybertruck is dead, and America will soon be free once again. God bless America, and God bless these United States.

#5838. Booze, Tobacco Together in Pregnancy May Worsen Baby's Facial Abnormalities

— Smaller face size, reduced growth, and dysmorphism worse with combined exposure, study shows

Prenatal exposure to both alcohol and tobacco smoke impacted the baby's facial development more than either alone, a longitudinal study from South Africa showed.

Three-dimensional facial scans at 1 month and 1 year of age showed the greatest differences in facial shape, size, and growth with co-exposure from early pregnancy compared with none or single-substance exposure, Michael Suttie, PhD, of the University of Oxford in England, and colleagues reported in Pediatrics.

For girls, tobacco plus alcohol exposure was associated with greater reductions in facial growth and measurements around the eyes. Craniofacial growth didn't catch up by age 1 for girls exposed continuously to both substances in utero. For boys, dual prenatal exposure was linked to reduced nasal growth, resulting in smaller noses at 1 year.

"Findings highlight tobacco's potentiating effect on alcohol-related craniofacial harm," the researchers wrote. "These findings highlight the importance of interventions targeting alcohol and smoking cessation during pregnancy to reduce teratogenic risk."

An estimated 5.4% of U.S. women smoke during pregnancy, which carries known risk of craniofacial developmental issues for the baby, including craniosynostosis and orofacial clefts. Some 9.8% of pregnant women globally consume alcohol, which can lead to the baby having facial characteristics such as nasal shortening, midline differences, midfacial hypoplasia, ocular differences, and mandibular anomalies aside from some of the most identifiable signs of fetal alcohol syndrome: a smooth philtrum above a short upper lip and shortened width from the inner to outer corner of the eye.

"Both teratogens are known to disrupt neural crest cell migration, survival, and differentiation, processes essential for the formation of midline facial structures, ocular features, and nasal morphology," the researchers noted. "Nicotine exposure potentially compounds this disruption [by alcohol] through oxidative stress, hypoxia, and nicotine-induced vasoconstriction, which may impair oxygen and nutrient delivery during critical periods of facial morphogenesis."

To look for evidence that the impact of these substances might be additive, Suttie's group examined the Safe Passage Study, a prospective cohort of more than 7,000 pregnancies in low socioeconomic communities in Cape Town, South Africa, which has one of the world's highest rates of alcohol use in pregnancy. The cohort largely comprised women of mixed ancestry, known as South African Colored.

Of the more than 7,000 participants in the study, the analysis homed in on the subset of 634 participants who had 3D facial imaging of their infants at age 1 month and 1 year and antenatal substance exposure data. Exclusion criteria included illicit drug use by the mother (including marijuana) and genetic diagnoses in infants.

Alcohol and smoking exposures had been assessed via interview at each prenatal visit, with frequency and quantity both captured. Continuous exposure was defined as exposure in the first trimester and any subsequent trimester. There were 152 infants categorized as without exposure, 48 with continuous alcohol-only exposure, 149 with continuous smoking-only exposure, 150 with continuous co-exposure, and 135 with continuous smoking and any alcohol use.

Continuous prenatal co-exposure to smoking and alcohol was associated with reduced facial size compared with both controls and single-exposure groups (P<0.05), driven by differences among girls. The single-exposure groups showed no differences compared with controls.

"Our findings of sex-specific dysmorphism are consistent with prior work suggesting differential vulnerability to prenatal alcohol exposure by sex," Suttie and colleagues noted.

Continuous co-exposure was associated with greater facial dysmorphism overall, with the biggest difference at 1 month (P<0.001) but still significant at 1 year (P<0.05). Consistent midline displacement was seen with co-exposure at both time points. More outward lateral movement of the inner canthi of the eye was also seen with co-exposure at both time points (P<0.05).

Limitations included the need to scan infants while sleeping, potential modification by maternal nutritional deficiencies, and unknown generalizability to populations with different genetic profiles.

"Our results contribute to a growing body of evidence on the harms of co-exposures, and we encourage clinicians and healthcare authorities to emphasize the potential harm of concurrent smoking and alcohol use during pregnancy," the researchers concluded.

#5837. How Can Europe Accelerate Electric Trucking?

Europe is having a hard time lately, with skyrocketing oil prices dampening economies. Fuel costs, particularly diesel, are prompting surging interest in truck electrification. Europe has been urging truck makers to move toward electric trucking, and they have responded with a variety of electric semi trucks from many manufacturers. Europe is a group of sovereign countries with many standards. The European Union is a political and economic union of 27 states in that area. It issued directives urging action and imposing penalties. In response to European Union directives, companies have formed EV100, a coalition of corporations responding to the need. In a recent story, Steve Hanley wrote about European electric truck makers’ difficulties expanding truck electrification. Here’s a quotation from the story: “In a letter to EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, of primary concern, in their estimation, is expanding the charging infrastructure for heavy-duty trucks in Europe.” There is no shortage of electric trucks in Europe. Expansion could go faster were it not for charging infrastructure. Manufacturers complain about “an alarming delay” in conditions needed to drive market uptake. For Europe, truck electrification is not working as well as in China, where over 90% of the world’s electric trucks reside. The differences between China and the EU show some reasons why truck electrification is slower in Europe. How did China succeed where the EU failed? China made electric trucks a freight system, not a vehicle category.

Power is a major factor in electric grid infrastructure. Charging electric trucks places demands on power. Peak power determines how much infrastructure is necessary. In grid planning, peak annual power determines how much capital equipment is necessary. Reducing peak power demand is a critical factor for electric truck infrastructure. Figure 1 shows one method of reducing power called route stuffing. It schedules departures on heavy traffic corridors at regularly spaced intervals. Corridors like ones between ports and warehouses are a target for those practices. These corridors often route trucks in a round trip chain. Filling routes with scheduled trips can reduce power demand compared to random trip scheduling. The article Battery Swap Uses Fewer Batteries Than You Think is devoted to methods of analysis and planning that can lead to lower peak power demand. There are other benefits to planning, such as greater truck load capacity from the same amount of batteries. Part of the solution to slow electric truck infrastructure development is to plan infrastructure and truck use practices to reduce the charging power burden. Given the pressing and enduring need due to the diesel fuel cost crisis, it is necessary to reprioritize grid power upgrade demands. Demands for data center power upgrades like transformers for substations should be re shuffled and prioritized toward the diesel crisis.

In two articles, Michael Barnard outlined the issues. Vehicles are not a transportation system. What does Europe have now? It has an EU Commission interacting with a coalition, EV100. The problem is, there are plenty of trucks available, but who is in charge of infrastructure? You can’t have electric trucks without means of charging, but as the coalition complains, “Significant improvements to charging infrastructure, a reduction in carbon dioxide based tolls, and a coherent policy framework are urgently needed.” There are so many stakeholders — including the commission, vehicles makers, and charging companies across multiple countries — that no one is in charge of infrastructure, and without it, nothing moves. It needs a unity of purpose and action.

If China is succeeding, why not adopt its strategy? Perhaps the answer is right in front of everyone’s nose. As Michael puts it, “the policy connects vehicles to corridors, depots, service areas, grids and freight use cases instead of treating sales targets as sufficient.” CATL offered Europe a system, not a vehicle. This is a “turn key” solution. It’s a well thought out system, including use of methods and practices, not an anything goes free-for-all. That kind of stability and predictability is what EV100 leaders are looking for. This is not a swap-or-nothing scenario. Different techniques apply to various use cases. Swap must be planned for high-use freight corridors and other proper applications. Swap trucks can also fast charge or slow charge, providing flexibility and a system of trucks that includes smaller trucks, not just semis.

What does all this have to do with Europe’s slowly advancing infrastructure? Simply put, electric trucks put heavy charging demands on the grid. Trucks can have megawatt-hour batteries that require megawatt power charging to charge in an hour. Reducing grid power demands can reduce grid infrastructure upgrade costs, and leverage capital investment toward faster implementation.

“The process of getting megawatt charging equipment connected to the grid can take several years, delaying deployment even where operators and infrastructure providers are ready to invest.” The need for megawatt charging equipment is reduced by accelerating swap network development instead of fixed battery trucks that must be charged by fast chargers. “Swaptopus is easy to misread as a quirky name for another electric-truck infrastructure project. It is a newly formed joint venture between Octopus Energy and CATL, created to develop automated battery-swapping hubs for heavy trucks across Europe.” Unlike the government of China that played a role in encouraging standards and cooperation in infrastructure, Europe has a looser arrangement between many countries with various standards. Europe is learning the slow, hard way where battery swapping is most needed.

Every truck application has different optimization. It means that there must be different approaches to fit freight operations in heavy traffic corridors. Quoting Michael Barnard, “Freight operators often run repeated routes between ports, factories, distribution centres and logistics hubs. Those patterns provide known traffic, known stopping points and relatively predictable electricity demand. A swap hub can be placed around an existing freight flow instead of hoping that enough unrelated trucks eventually pass through.”

Freight corridors are a scenario made to order for battery swap. Real trucking solutions include a mix of vehicle and infrastructure types — from small, local delivery, to large, long-haul freight; and from slow, overnight charging, to medium power charging and battery swap — all used in concert to accelerate heavy truck electrification. With a wide variety of charging options, and vehicles and charging use cases targeted in coordination to avoid peak power demands, the path forward is eased. School buses don’t need expensive high-power fast charging. Lower-power chargers can do the trick. Local delivery can use a mix of overnight and medium power charging. Heavy truck dispatch must be more carefully coordinated to avoid peak demand and grid upgrade costs. A mix of medium-power charging and swap stations along with planned use cases can successfully lower electric freight power needs and transport system capital expenses to speed transport electrification.

Transformation and conversion of diesel freight systems to electric requires coordination and planning between government agencies and coalitions of corporations, cities, government agencies, and planners. Transportation is a system basic to societies and economics. Coordination between groups at all levels results in practices, use cases, and infrastructure that produce benefits for all. Grid expansion and construction can take years. In order for Europe to implement truck freight electrification, more structure and planning is needed to minimize grid power requirements, speed implementation, and maximize capital investment results. Transportation system, practices, and infrastructure must be planned for optimum results.

#5836. At $18,900, Is This Incredibly Low-Mileage 1986 Chrysler LeBaron Town & Country A Woody You Would Buy?

With just 3,800 miles on the clock, today's Nice Price or No Dice LeBaron Town & Country is a true time capsule of '80s glory. It even has a bench seat in the front! Now priced about 30% more than when it was new, we'll have to decide whether it's worth it to feel the MTV-era vibes.

With the introduction of the Prius in the late 1990s, Toyota rewrote the meaning of a "hybrid auto." Before the Prius mated electric and internal combustion motors for power, a hybrid auto typically meant an American engine in a European car. The Sunbeam Tiger with its British-built body and Ford 289 was a hybrid. So too were the Iso Rivolta and the clutch of Bizzarrini, which sported Chevy small-block power.

The 2013 Cadillac Escalade we looked at on Thursday is a hybrid in the modern sense, featuring a gearbox employing two electric motors to aid the V8 engine in both driving the SUV and keeping its high-voltage battery full of electrons. That was, and still is, a fiddly system with a number of known failure points. On top of that, our Escalade already had 140K under its belt, so those failures could be expected at any given time. Those factors led to warnings in the comments and eventually, a 65% 'No Dice' loss for the Caddy's $11,995 asking price.

In the 1933 novel "Lost Horizon" by James Hilton, a small group of Westerners survives a plane crash high in a remote, uncharted part of the Himalayas. There, they discover a lamasery—Shangri-La—which seemingly has magical properties that slow aging among its inhabitants. This comes at a high cost: the inhabitants are trapped there, because leaving means rapidly aging and dying. I know, bummer.

Today's 1986 Chrysler LeBaron Town & Country looks like it was just magically freed from some mystical Shangri-La, as it appears in as-new, almost entirely original condition and has less than 4,000 miles on the clock. How did this come to be? The seller has a succinct recap in the ad:

Back in 1986 a man bought his wife the finest station wagon Chrysler produced, this LeBaron Town & Country TURBO wagon. She only drove it 1500 miles before parking it in the garage when she became ill, and ultimately passed. The car ended up in climate controlled storage at a Chrysler dealer for 30 years. Then during Covid it was brought back to life with a new gas tank, driven a couple hundred miles and ended up on consignment at World Wide Autos in Colorado.

The current owner bought the car four years ago, brought it to Georgia, and replaced all the rubber bits, fluids, and the non-working factory stereo. Other than those updates, this K Car is claimed to be just as it left the factory.

This Town & Country has the goods, too. An unexpected decal on the hood announces the engine: a 2.2-liter Chrysler four with fuel injection and a Garrett T03 turbocharger. The motor was factory-rated at 146 horsepower and 168 pound-feet of torque, which might not seem like all that and a bag of chips today, but back in the mid-'80s it was pretty impressive.

Befitting this car's role as a Town & Country cruiser, the motor is mated to a three-speed TorqueFlite automatic which drives the front wheels.

According to the ad, the car is 100% roadworthy and even has working R12 A/C. Before the current owner took possession, a previous owner replaced the gas tank. That, the rubber, and the radio are apparently the only hard bits of the car that aren't factory original. That makes this LeBaron a total time capsule, and the seller boasts it's a hit at many local car shows.

Of course, this also has the look that anyone with an "I HEART THE '80s" tattoo will simply gush over. There's an old joke about a traveler stopping into a bar in the South and asking what kind of music they play there, to which the bartender replies, "Oh, we got both types: country AND western." This LeBaron is similarly a Town & Country model, meaning it has the faux woodgrain paneling down its flanks emulating the classic Town & Country Chryslers of the 1940s. That's in amazing condition with no apparent fading or damage. Under that is a coat of elegant black paint that looks to be simple, single-stage. Chrome wire wheel covers complete the picture.

There's more old-school goodness in the cabin, as it features a wide split-bench seat in the front, clean gray cloth upholstery, and a low center tunnel afforded by the FWD layout that offers a ton of foot room.

This is a high-end K-car, so it has power windows and locks, cruise control, a tilt wheel, and the aforementioned A/C. The modern Sony stereo is a bit of a letdown, but is probably more useful than the non-working original, even if it spoils the overall throwback experience.

This LeBaron comes with a clean title, and the seller suggests that while museums are welcome to snap it up, the wagon should really be enjoyed on the road. That, of course, means adding to its miles, which takes away one of the car's unique ownership aspects. Maybe put it on a flatbed and drive it around so you can enjoy the experience without ruining that uber-low mileage fame.

Whatever the choice, we'll now have to consider LeBaron's $18,900 asking price. That's a good bit higher than the around $12K it cost when new, but inflation has taken its toll, and honestly, where are you going to find another one in this condition and spec? Supply and demand is one of the first things they teach you in Econ 101.

What do you think about this LeBaron and that $18,900 asking? Do you feel like a buyer should be resigned to pay that price given the car's rarity and condition? Or is that too much even if this LeBaron offers both Town AND Country?

#5835. Trump Is Gonna Cave On Offshore Wind In 5…4…3…

…JK! US President Donald Trump will never cry surrender in the war against offshore wind turbines. The President was burned once before, when a wind farm arose in Aberdeen Bay in Scotland, within view of a Trump-branded golf course back in the early 2000’s. Never again! The President has taken extreme measures to prevent such blight from tainting the shores of the United States. Nevertheless, scores of the pesky oversized pinwheels have already eluded the Trump chopper, and many more are on the way.

The latest news concerns CVOW, the 2.6-gigwatt Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project under the wing of the leading utility Dominion. As the name of the project indicates, CVOW sits in the Atlantic Ocean about 24 nautical miles (28 land miles) off the coast of Virginia Beach, Virginia.

CVOW began taking shape during Trump’s first turn around the Oval Office, and construction was well under way when his second term began on January 20, 2025.

Immediately upon taking office, Trump abruptly suspended the offshore wind lease program administered by the Department of the Interior. He also ordered spurious re-reviews of offshore projects that were already in the permitting pipeline, and he had the Department of Justice administer a legally questionable buy-back program to prevent activity from stirring among other lease holders. In addition, he had the Interior Department issue multiple emergency orders aimed at stopping five offshore projects off the coasts of Rhode Island, Connecticut, New Jersey, New York, Maryland, and Massachusetts, where construction work was already well under way.

So far, though, only one part of the effort has stuck. Last year a federal judge affirmed that any President, Trump or not, has the authority to stop issuing new offshore leases. However, the same judge decided there is no blanket authority to suspend offshore leases that are already in the permitting process. The buy-back program is also in litigation, with critics raising questions about the funds used to pay off lease holders among other issues.

Additionally,  the Interior Department failed to convince multiple federal judges that the emergency orders had any merit. Work has continued on all five Atlantic coast projects, including CVOW.

CVOW began delivering its first kilowatts to shore in March, and Dominion recapped its progress on the wind farm in its Q3 report on October 30. As handily summarized by the news organization Maritime Executive, the project currently clocks in at 85% complete. All of the main turbine components — nacelles, towers, and blades — for the wind farm’s 176 offshore wind turbines have been fabricated. Forty-four have been fully installed so far. With a 45th coming any day now, the wind farm currently hosts 640 megawatts out of the 2,600 megawatt total.

Since Trump declared an “Energy Emergency” in January of 2025, it’s fair to ask why he has spent so much time, energy and taxpayer dollars to crush an entire domestic energy industry. After all, if one was not reading too closely between the lines of the declaration, the new energy policy is little more than a rehash of former President Barack Obama’s “All Of The Above” energy policy. As further embellished by Energy Secretary Chris Wright, the new version specifically taps multiple zero and low-emission energy resources for support including nuclear energy, biomass, hydropower, and geothermal energy, just like Obama did, along the emerging field of marine energy, which was barely a speck on the horizon while Obama was in office.

Energy storage, and the critical minerals needed in the clean tech industry, have also been gathered up in a Trumpian embrace.

Conspicuously absent, however, are the two most abundant, economical, and easily accessible domestic energy resources, namely, wind and solar.

If there really was an energy emergency…oh, never mind! Despite Trump’s complaints, offshore wind is a mature industry with a vigorous supply global supply chain and support equipment, as deftly illustrated by the CVOW project. In the October 30 report, Dominion noted that it takes only about two days for an offshore construction vessel to install a wind turbine on its foundation.

While the offshore wind construction timetable is subject to weather delays, Dominion also stated that the project is on schedule — despite any further delays related to last year’s stop-work order.

Speaking of the stop-work order, CVOW was conspicuously excluded from previous rounds of stop-work orders impacting the four other Atlantic coast wind farms under construction in 2025. If you’re guessing that Virginia’s Republican Governor, Glenn Youngkin, had a hand in that decision, drop a note in the discussion thread. Youngkin publicly supported the CVOW project but he was term-limited out of office last year. A stop-work order would have put an embarrassing crimp in his next-step political plans. The order came down only after Election Day 2025, after the Democratic candidate, Abigail Spanberger, won the post.

In a classic case of karma biting back, CVOW is a  more efficient and economical project than initially envisioned. A round of delays during Trump’s first term in office gave Dominion an opportunity to redesign the project with next-generation wind turbines. Those delays also enabled Dominion to take advantage of a new generation of turbine installation vessels that are purpose-built to cut offshore construction costs.

The results speak for themselves. In its October 30 report, Dominion indicated that CVOW costs were still consistent with its capital budget, even accounting for the cost of last year’s stop-work order and costs related to Trump’s tariff wars.

“The estimates on the levelized cost of energy (LCOE) also continue to fall,” Maritime Executive summarized. “After starting with a forecasted range of $80-$90 per MWh, and adjustments for changes after the change in administrations, they have lowered the LCOE to $62, down from an estimate of $83 presented in August” (LCOE is a calculation that provides a common ground for comparing costs among different forms of power generation).

Maritime Executive further reported that Dominion expects to save its ratepayers about $5 billion on fuel over the first 10 years of operation.

Trump’s war on wind has also petered out elsewhere. The Revolution Wind project off the coasts of Connecticut and Massachusetts has also been a target of  multiple stop-work orders over the past two years, with the latest hammer coming down just two weeks ago, when the 704-megawatt wind farm was almost complete.

Revolution Wind is now fully operational, joining the nearby Vineyard Wind project which also endured multiple attacks from Trump. As reported by public radio station WBUR, the savings from Revolution Wind is expected to ripple out through New England, saving $500 million for ratepayers in the region every year.

As for the domestic offshore wind industry writ large, the US lost thousands of onshore supply chain jobs all around the US in addition to job losses related to portside and offshore operation. However, the trade organization Oceantic Network is already prepping for a comeback. “The road to recovery for the embattled American offshore wind industry starts today with a new political mandate to tackle the affordability crisis,” Oceantic President and CEO Liz said in a public statement celebrating the Republican Party’s crushing defeat in the 202y midterm elections.

Photo: The offshore wind construction vessel Charybdis can install wind turbines at Virginia’s CVOW wind farm in just two days (cropped; courtesy of Dominion via CleanTechnica archive).

#5833. What Car Screams 'I'm Divorced'?

There are few bigger changes in a person's life than when they get divorced, which is probably why it's not too uncommon for a divorce to be rung in with the purchase of a new car — provided you didn't get taken to the cleaners by your spouse's far-superior lawyers. You've got a new life, new priorities and even a new way you'd like to have yourself represented to the world, and that idea is what brings me to today's question.

I want to know what car screams "I'm divorced!" What car lets everybody know that it didn't work out between you and the missus (or mister)? While technically, yes, any car can be a divorced person's car, that's really not what I'm looking for today. I want to know what car leaves zero doubt that someone has to sit separately from his ex-wife at school functions for fear that there could be an incident.

I'm not going to be too much of a stickler about the car you pick, either. It can be new or used, because classic cars definitely have an air of divorce about them, too, and so do cheap used cars — especially if divorce court didn't go your way.

For my pick for this question, I'm going with something new to keep it interesting. The answer to which car screams "I'm divorced!" is the Dodge Charger Sixpack R/T — the Hurricane inline-six-powered Dodge muscle car. Specifically, it has to be the two-door coupe, because you're only seeing the kids on weekends, anyway. Why do you need easy access to the rear seats? Exactly.

The car has everything the modern divorced man needs: throwback looks to a time when their hair wasn't thinning, a big enough trunk to hold the toys they're going to bribe their kids with, and even a reasonable starting price at $51,990, including destination. Add in the 420 horsepower it produces and the fact it'll do zero to 60 mph in 4.6 seconds (fast enough to outrun your demons and the alimony payments), and you've got a winner on your hands. Of course, you could always go for the more expensive Charger Sixpack Scat Pack, but court was never going to let you off the hook that easily, so you've got to save where you can.

Anyway, that's enough out of me. How about you all head on down below and let your fellow Jalops know what cars scream "I'm divorced"? As always, I'll love you more if you tell me why you made your pick.

#5831. Ferrari Is Unstoppable Right Now

Good morning! It's Friday, November 6, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition, Ferrari is making even more money than it expected as the rich continue to spend big, Audi could boost the size of its planned U.S. auto plant, battery electric vehicle market share just hit a new record in Europe and Mitsubishi looks to the Pajero to turn things around.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

It's true that you and I don't have any money, but do you know who does? Ferrari buyers. Lots of it, too. That's why the Italian supercar maker raised its forecast for this year's results after beating estimates on core profits and revenue in the third quarter. If only the F1 team could be as successful.

Ferrari pointed to sales of higher-margin vehicles and lucrative optional extras added to its vehicles as reasons for the company's strong financial performance. Order books now reach into 2028, and as we reported earlier this week, the Luce EV is already sold out for all of 2027. From Reuters:

Ferrari guided for its ‌adjusted ⁠earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) to rise to at least €3 billion ($3.36 billion) in 2026, versus a previous forecast for a result of at least €2.97 billion.

The company also nudged up its forecast for this year's net revenue, while guiding for an industrial free cash flow generation of up to €1.65 billion in 2026.

Ferrari's ​forecast upgrade was based on ​stronger-than-expected personalisations – those finishing ⁠touches customers request at extra cost to make their cars better suited to their individual tastes, led by the 296 Speciale model family – as ​well as softer currency headwinds and its current second place in the Formula ​1 Championship.

In the third quarter, Ferrari's adjusted EBITDA rose 12% to €753 million, topping a €739 million analyst consensus in a Reuters poll.

Sales of the €3.6 million limited-edition F80 supercar improved Ferrari's product mix in the ⁠third ​quarter and its result in the period, the company said, ​despite another drop in overall car shipments, as it presses ahead with a planned model changeover.

Between July and September, Ferrari says it shipped 3,368 vehicles, which is actually 33 fewer than the same period last year, but it doesn't seem that the slight discrepancy mattered much.

Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna added that Ferrari still has two more model launches coming this year, and he's "sure" clients will be "super happy" about them. Of course, while clients seem to be happy about the Luce, folks who cannot afford one seemed to be very upset. It remains to be seen if that history will repeat itself.

Audi is gearing up to build a massive $4 billion assembly plant in Macon, Georgia, and even though it won't open until the early 2030s, the German automaker is already considering a second phase that'll add $3 billion in costs and an extra 3,000 workers when it's completed in 3033, according to documents released by the Mid-Georgia Gateway Development Authority.

Georgia is giving Audi the 1,500-acre site, providing $458 million in tax incentives and over $120 million in grants for infrastructure, rail improvements, environmental sites, remediation and construction. That's not all, there's another $430 million coming Audi's way for water, road improvements, utility issues and workforce training and recruitment. It's a pretty sweet deal for Audi, I'll tell you what. Of course, that's all on top of the tariff relief President Trump promised Audi to help secure the plant's future. From Reuters:

Two ​sources briefed on ​the matter said ⁠Audi has pushed the US to reduce the 15% tariffs it pays on imports from the EU ​to 7.5%, but that the US Commerce Department was ​expected to ⁠agree to around 10%.

The tariff relief program aims to prod automakers to add US production or other investments, the sources added.

Trump's tariffs on ⁠autos, steel, ​aluminum and parts cost Audi around €1.2 billion ($1.4 ​billion) last year as it imports all its vehicles for the US market from Europe ​or Mexico.

Currently, Audi's plan is for the plant to pump out 200,000 SUVs per year and employ 4,500 workers, so adding another 3,000 workers is no small chunk. There's no word on how much capacity would be increased, but I'd have to assume it's going to be sizable.

Battery-electric vehicles took 34% of new car registrations in 12 European markets in October, which, if you're keeping track at home, is a record share. While that may sound like good news, it's causing a bit of a headache for automakers as it strains supply and squeezes margins, as the surge came faster than some OEMs' battery supply and cost structures could comfortably handle. In Germany, the country where the largest automaker is Europe's are located, BEVs hit a record 37%. That's sort of wild to think about. From Automotive News:

BEV sales in the 12 markets rose 57 percent during the month to reach a 34 percent market share, up from 22.4 percent in October 2025, according to an Automotive News Europe analysis. BEV penetration averaged 21 percent in the first half of 2026 before steadily increasing through the third quarter and reaching 33 percent in September.

In the first 10 months of 2026, BEV sales increased 44 percent to 2.63 million vehicles, while the overall market grew 6 percent. As a result, BEV market share rose to 27 percent from 20 percent a year earlier.

Germany was among the fastest-growing EV markets in October. BEV registrations rose 79 percent to 94,086 vehicles, accounting for a record 37 percent of monthly sales. Through October, battery-electric vehicles represented 28.2 percent of the German market, up nearly 10 percentage points from 2025.

In the U.K., BEVs captured 32.7 percent of registrations in October, up 6.5 percentage points from the same month in 2025. Through October, BEVs held a 27 percent share of the market, compared with 22 percent a year earlier.

France also remained a strong BEV market. Battery-electric registrations totaled 61,958 in October, giving BEVs a 41.5 percent market share, only slightly below September's record 41.7 percent. Through October, BEVs accounted for 32 percent of French registrations, compared with 20 percent in 2025.

Several smaller markets continued to post some of Europe's highest EV penetration rates. BEVs accounted for 55 percent of registrations in the Netherlands, 51 percent in Sweden and 49 percent in Belgium.

There are bottlenecks to deal with for some automakers, though.

Mercedes-Benz said its electric GLC midsize SUV is sold out in Europe for the remainder of 2026 because of exceptionally strong demand. For some configurations, customers placing orders now may have to wait until the third or fourth quarter of 2027 for delivery.

Volkswagen Group has also reported stronger-than-expected demand for its new entry-level EVs. Orders for the ID Polo exceeded 30,000 by early September, while the Cupra Raval accumulated more than 51,000 reservations. The automaker said demand could lead to extended waiting times for some versions.

Automakers are also grappling with the financial consequences of the accelerating shift to BEVs.

During VW Group's third-quarter earnings call on Oct. 29, CFO Arno Antlitz said the company's BEV transition is occurring faster than anticipated. The group's order book now consists of about 40 percent BEVs, a level it had originally expected to reach only in 2029.

Till Conrad, head of marketing at Toyota Europe, said battery-electric vehicles still generate lower margins than hybrids and conventional vehicles, although falling battery costs should help close the gap.

This seems like a real "damned if you do, damned if you don't" situation. I'm not really sure what the solution is, because I'm a goofus, but I can certainly understand why automakers have fought so vehemently against the transition to EVs.

Mitsubishi cut its full-year profit forecast, saying the war in the Middle East is hurting sales and driving up costs. Now, the Japanese automaker says it expects its operating profit to decline 7.3% — a reversal from a previously predicted expansion. From Automotive News:

Mitsubishi's revision has operating profit declining to ¥70 billion ($444.8 million) in the current fiscal year ending March 31, from ¥75.5 billion ($479.8 million) the year before.

In August, the company predicted profit would grow 19 percent to ¥90 billion ($571.9 million).

Mitsubishi also downgraded its net income outlook to be flat with the previous year. It had earlier expected net income to more than double in the current fiscal year.

In announcing financial results, COO Keisuke Kishiura said Middle East disruption will dent full-year operating profit by ¥45 billion ($285.9 million), including lost sales and higher transportation and raw material costs. The reversal shows how the lingering conflict continues to affect auto industry costs and demand, while Mitsubishi lags rivals in hybrids and electric vehicles.

Mitsubishi dialed back its outlook despite announcing a 75 percent surge in operating profit and narrower net loss for the fiscal second quarter ended Sept. 30.

The automaker lowered its global sales forecast to 764,000 vehicles for its current fiscal year due to declining volume in Southeast Asia, Australia, North America and Europe.

The new guidance represents a 4.1 percent decline from the previous year.

Mitsubishi had earlier forecast global sales to increase 7.5 percent to 857,000 vehicles.

Mitsubishi expects North American deliveries to fall 7 percent to 154,000 vehicles, European sales to decline 5 percent to 40,000 and Southeast Asia to lose 12 percent to 216,000.

Mitsubishi sees Japan sales increasing 11 percent to 136,000 vehicles.

Mitsubishi is hoping the newly reintroduced Pajero will boost sales. The automaker has already taken 9,000 orders worldwide for its new off-road SUV, meant to take on the Toyota Land Cruiser. Its goal is to sell 10,000 of them by the end of the current fiscal year, which ends on March 31, 2027. It's already on sale in Thailand — where it's built — and will hit dealerships in Japan and Australia in December. There's still no word on whether or not it'll come Stateside, but we can keep our fingers crossed.

#5829. These Risky Car Purchases Ended Up Being Way More Reliable For Our Readers Than Most People Would Assume

Somehow, despite buying a used 2006 Ducati Monster with more than 20,000 miles on the odometer and having done no pre-purchase inspection, my bike ended up being pretty darn reliable. I had a feeling it would be based on the way the previous owner had cared for and modified it, and they'd clearly loved riding it, but other than replacing the front fork seals, I didn't have to do any work to it the entire time I lived in the Los Angeles metro area. Ducati may be the Ferrari of motorcycles, but it sure didn't feel like it based on running costs.

If you know motorcycles, you know that's because Ducati Monsters are pretty darn reliable. Non-motorcycle people tend to see the bright paint, wild styling, and Italian heritage and assume Monsters are in the shop just as often as an '80s Lamborghini. That got me thinking — surely, I can't be the only one who's owned vehicles that ended up being more reliable and cheaper to own than other people tend to assume.

So I asked for your examples, and boy, let me tell you. I did not need the encouragement some of your stories are giving me. Despite the horror stories, part of me wants to replace the Fiat with a BMW i8, and I'm going to have to get incredibly lucky if I'm going to pull that off without ruining my finances. But that doesn't mean I didn't enjoy the encouragement. Let's take a look at some of the most popular answers.

My 2014 Panamera 4 has been 100% rock-solid. I have done only routine maintenance except. Maintance isn't always cheap HOWEVER the car is one of the most reliable cars I have ever owned and now that I do my own oil changes (and might try brakes when they are due), the cost will drop even more.

Second has been the two Abarths I have owned (still have my 2014 that I autocross). The internet makes it seem like these cars will break-down as much as the old Fiat 124's but these cars have never let me down. In fact, working on my Abarth is extremely easy. There is a huge fanbase so finding videos or advice on modifying or DIY maintenance on these cars is easy. I push the Abarth all the time and it takes it.

Fun and reliable don't need to be an oxymoron.

I've been daily driving an 87 Alfa Romeo Milano for 7 years now. It's been off the road maybe 2 weeks total during that time, sometimes for optional upgrades.

I've heard endless thoughts, jokes, etc about the infamous "Alfa reliability", all from people who have never owned an Alfa. I get my laughs from my neighbor, who has often given his thoughts. He has a Toyota pickup of the same era that has driven 7000 less miles than the Alfa over our decade as neighbors due to constant issues.

2011 WRX right from the factory. Deep in the middle of the whole ring land fiasco. Here we are in 2026 and it's still standing, 170k+ later.

I bought a 2017 Dodge Durango R/T red on red. My wife liked the colors and I got V8 out of it. I traded a 2013 Nissan Pathfinder on it, that was already on a second CVT replacement under warranty. Dodge had a reputation and still does and I fully expected it to not last very long being a Chrysler product, but I bought it as a dealer demo/manager's car with about 5-6k miles in August 2017 and it now has over 203k miles. Never left me stranded. The one time it came close is when my local mechanic messed up valve cover gasket replacedment (at around 175k miles) and it started spitting oil, but that's not the car's fault. Still made it home and the shop stood behind their work and replaced it again for free. At this point, I am afraid of getting a new one, because post Covid quality went down the drain.

We bought a 2013 Fiat 500 Pop to be my daughter's first car. We got it in 2017 with 1300 miles on it.

She drove it for years, and we sold it with 87k virtually trouble free miles. About the only thing that went wrong with it was the driver's arm rest broke.

Everything else was just typical maintenance.

In my case, and without any doubts, my FIAT 500 Abarth. 14 years with absolutely no problem. none. A Fix It Again Tony they said.

My dad has now screwed around twice and gotten a secondhand CPO Maserati Quattroporte, and both have held up remarkably well. A 2015 lasted him from 2018-2025, and I'm fairly certain he made it to 100k only needing a significant brake job around the 70k mile mark. Now he's driving a '22 he bought last year. I think this one will go on a bit longer because its better in every way. The '15 felt pretty dated towards the end because, shoot, it was Chrysler interior equipment from the early 2010's. Mechanicals still seemed solid when he got rid of it.

All that said, the depreciation curve across those 7 years he drove the first was not friendly. Want to say he got in for $50k and trade it in in the high teens. Still though, you would think buying a used Maserati is a much worse decision than its turned out to be.

I bought a 100k mile '07 Quattroporte about a year and a half ago, and it has been a dream. I've put about 20k (I have a long commute) on it since then. I have had exactly ZERO issues or concerns with it. It just goes when and where I ask it to. That said, I was VERY particular when looking for one, but still got it for under $10k. The previous owner had owned it for 16 years and had all maintenance records. The only thing I've had done so far is having the bumpers and mirrors repainted to take care of the normal clearcoat issues. The backup sensors don't work, though. Maybe I'll fix that someday.

2016 GTI bought new. After dailying – and maintaining – a 944 from 2000-2013 I was deeply skeptical of another car from Ze Germans. But I observed plenty of "VW isn't like it was in the 90s" reports and risked it – knock on wood, it's been very reliable – enough so that I got a 2024 Tiguan (and a tune right off the bat) without worrying about it.

Our 2000 Porsche Boxster has given us very little issue in the 11 years we've owned it. We've replaced the water pump and the air oil separator and that's it besides regular maintenance. It regularly gets driven hard as well. Even some autox work.

1978 Fiat 124 Sport Spider. Our family has had it 20 years, we're the third owner, and I knew all of the stories but it was just so pretty and rust free. It's been a great car and it cranked and got me to work one morning when my Honda Accord wouldn't.

I bought a supercharged BMW e46 m3 sight unseen in 2019 and it's performed flawlessly as a drift car ever since. Every spring I get the oil analyized and every time the report comes back great so I keep ripping it. Rod bearing failure in these cars are over exaggerated.

#5828. America’s New Shipbuilding Orders Are Expensive Bets on Fossil Freight

South Korea’s Hanwha Group owns the Philadelphia shipyard that has become a centerpiece of Washington’s attempt to rebuild American commercial shipbuilding. Its Hanwha Ocean and Hanwha Systems subsidiaries acquired the US yard in December 2024. The investment creates and sustains American production capacity and jobs while transferring shipbuilding expertise, technology and training from South Korea to US workers. The facility is in America, but its corporate ownership remains South Korean. The company’s published orderbook, however, tells a more complicated story: two liquefied natural gas carriers, four firm orders for oil and chemical tankers, and options for another six tankers. Three LNG-fueled container ships ordered by Matson in 2022 predate the current administration. The newer LNG and tanker orders come from Hanwha’s own shipping affiliates. They can help restart production, but buying ships from another company in the same group does not demonstrate that independent shipowners will pay US construction prices.

The price gap is difficult to dismiss. Kinder Morgan’s January 2026 investor presentation estimates that a new medium-range Jones Act tanker would cost more than $240 million and require a long-term charter above $115,000 per day to justify construction. The existing charter market was around $90,000 per day. Kinder Morgan operates 16 tankers, with its fleet fully utilized, yet the gap between current charter revenue and the cost of a replacement vessel remains substantial. High utilization establishes a need for shipping services; it does not establish a financeable order for a new American-built tanker at today’s prices.

Coastal petroleum shipping also competes with other domestic infrastructure. A 2025 report to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission estimated moving gasoline from Houston to New York Harbor at under 8 cents per gallon by pipeline, about 20 cents by ship, and roughly 35 cents by rail. These illustrative route costs do not cover every destination, and tankers remain essential where pipelines are unavailable. They do show why expensive new tankers cannot count on charter customers accepting whatever price domestic construction requires. Longer term, the International Energy Agency estimates that electric vehicles displaced 1.7 million barrels of oil per day worldwide in 2025 and could displace about 5 million by 2030 under its policy scenarios. That does not mean US tanker demand vanishes, but fleet investment must account for changes in the cargo market over several decades.

LNG export carriers have a more plausible near-term growth market, although their prospects are different from the prospects of LNG-fueled container ships. US gas exports may expand, and LNG tankers will be needed to carry them. The commercial test for a US-built LNG carrier is whether it can win an arm’s-length contract against established Korean, Japanese and Chinese shipyards. Hanwha’s plan to train Philadelphia workers through its Korean shipyards can strengthen US industrial capability, and affiliated orders can provide an initial production run. The central uncertainty is whether independent buyers will still choose these ships once the group’s internal demand and any cargo preference are removed.

A broader domestic vessel market already exists. US-flag Great Lakes freighters carried 71.3 million tons in 2025, much of it iron ore, limestone, cement, coal and other bulk materials. Those cargo flows will change as steelmaking and energy systems evolve, while ferry services, harbour vessels, inland cargo craft and multipurpose ships will still require renewal. Battery-electric and hybrid-electric propulsion offer practical options on routes with manageable energy requirements and reliable charging access. Large, long-distance bulk ships need a more selective technology assessment, rather than an assumption that every vessel can run on batteries.

Recent projects demonstrate what a committed customer can contribute to ship economics. CMA CGM, Nike and Gemadept launched an electric inland barge in Vietnam for a 180-kilometre round trip. Nike agreed to fill 90% of its capacity for eight years, helping justify a vessel reportedly costing about twice as much as its diesel equivalent. A dedicated charging installation and renewable electricity form part of the service. That is a commercially structured freight proposition, with its higher capital cost supported by contracted utilization and expected operating savings.

Electric propulsion does not cure the American shipbuilding cost problem by itself. Washington State’s three new hybrid-electric ferries carry a $714.5 million shipbuilding contract, and the state’s estimate including additional equipment and other program expenses is approximately $1.15 billion. Construction has started; the ferries are not yet in service. The path to a productive shipbuilding industry still runs through standardized designs, modular fabrication, trained workers, repeat orders, reliable delivery and falling labor-hours per vessel. It would be a mistake to treat electrification as a substitute for manufacturing reform.

Hanwha’s South Korean capital and know-how could contribute to that reform by developing US suppliers and production skills that serve several vessel classes. That is a meaningful way to rebuild domestic capability even though the parent company remains foreign-owned. Its progress should ultimately be measured by independent repeat customers, improving construction costs and commercially competitive vessels, rather than affiliated orders or investment announcements. A US maritime strategy anchored to the fossil-fuel cargoes of today risks missing a growing opportunity to build modern domestic vessels for the freight, port and ferry services of tomorrow.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Hanwha’s orders, Kinder Morgan’s tanker economics and the market for repeatable electric and hybrid maritime construction. It follows my earlier analysis of the Jones Act’s shipbuilding capacity gap.

#5827. Lumateperone Brings Rapid Relief in Bipolar Mania

— The atypical antipsychotic improved symptoms within 3 days

Lumateperone (Caplyta) rapidly improved symptoms of acute mania associated with bipolar I disorder, a phase III trial showed.

Among 351 patients with or without mixed features, lumateperone demonstrated superiority over placebo in reducing the Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) total score by day 22 (least squares mean difference -3.7, 95% CI -5.61 to -1.86, P<0.0001), with significant differences noted by day 3 and maintained from week 1 onward, reported Roger S. McIntyre, MD, of the University of Toronto, and colleagues.

Meeting the key secondary endpoint, the atypical antipsychotic also led to greater improvement in overall illness severity, demonstrating superiority over placebo in change in Clinical Global Impression-Severity (CGI-S) score (least squares mean difference -0.4, 95% CI -0.58 to -0.17, P=0.0003).

The study was presented at the Neuroscience Education Institute (NEI) Fall Congress in Colorado Springs, Colorado.

"The overall clinical meaningfulness was not only observed rapidly on day 3, which was the second day post-treatment, but also response rates that translate into a number needed to treat of 5, indicating clinical relevance," McIntyre told MedPage Today.

"These efficacy findings alongside low rates of treatment-emergent adverse events and discontinuation rates due to adverse events, similar to placebo, underscore the clinical utility of lumateperone and why it would be a preferred treatment in adults presenting with mania with or without mixed features," he said.

This was the second pivotal phase III study evaluating lumateperone for acute bipolar mania. Its findings replicate and reinforce results from an identically designed sister trial reported in September at Psych Congress.

The once-daily, oral antipsychotic is not currently approved for the treatment of manic episodes associated with bipolar I disorder, but is approved for adults with bipolar depression (as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy with lithium or valproate), for schizophrenia, and as an adjunctive therapy with antidepressants for major depressive disorder.

While the mechanism of action of lumateperone is unknown, its efficacy could be mediated through a combination of antagonist activity at central serotonin 5-HT2A receptors and partial agonist activity at central dopamine D2 receptors.

"With respect to existing knowledge of lumateperone, these data establish the efficacy of lumateperone across the mood spectrum," said McIntyre.

"Notwithstanding options available for the treatment of bipolar mania with and without mixed features in adults, there remains a need for treatments that are rapidly efficacious with meaningful improvements for what effectively is a medical emergency, that is, bipolar mania," he noted.

Michael Thase, MD, of the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, previously underscored in a statement from the drugmaker that "mania is among the most dangerous and worrisome phases of bipolar disorder, and treating it effectively takes more than partial or temporary relief of symptoms; it means bringing the episode itself under control as quickly as possible."

For the double-blind trial, eligible patients diagnosed with bipolar I disorder and an acute manic episode with or without mixed features (symptoms of mania or hypomania along with symptoms of depression) according to DSM-5-TR criteria were randomized 1:1 to receive 3 weeks of either lumateperone 42 mg or placebo. Treatment began in an inpatient setting, with patients eligible for discharge to outpatient care after week 2.

Average patient age was 46.1 years, and 56.1% were men. About 44% experienced five or more lifetime manic episodes, and a third were diagnosed with mixed features. Both groups had severe mania at baseline according to mean YMRS scores.

Nearly twice as many participants in the lumateperone group achieved treatment response, defined as a 50% or greater reduction in YMRS score (43.9% vs 23.7%, P<0.0001). More patients on treatment also met qualifications for remission, defined as a YMRS score of 12 or less (25.4% vs 16.4%, P=0.0330).

"The efficacy, tolerability, and safety record accords with what we have seen previously in bipolar depression and schizophrenia," said McIntyre.

The most common treatment-emergent adverse events with lumateperone versus placebo were dizziness (10.4% vs 1.7%), dry mouth (5.8% vs 1.1%), and somnolence (5.2% vs 1.7%). Discontinuation rates due to adverse events were low (4.0% vs 3.4%).

#5825. As Jackery Inventory Sells Out, Are Portable Batteries Set To Take Off?

I recently wrote reviews of the new Jackery HomePower 1000 Plus v2 and Explorer 100D. A few days later, a connection with Jackery messaged me that their Black Friday/Cyber Monday products had largely sold out. Just three days after launching on November 1. This includes 1000, 2000, 3600 and 5000 portable power and solar generator models. Additional models have sold out since then or will likely sell out soon. The recently launched Explorer 100D is still available in limited quantities at Walmart and Costco.

While Jackery will still take orders for Black Friday/Cyber Monday sales, most models currently listed for purchase will be on a preorder basis. Customers should check estimated delivery dates. Some restocking is expected in late November, although broader inventory availability may not recover until early next year.

While much of America was recovering from Halloween and election victory parties, portable batteries were selling out. This wasn’t the result of limited supply, but rather a massive, unanticipated increase in demand.

Between October 19th  and 26th, Jackery retail sales increased 755% at Costco, 106% at Walmart, 297% at The Home Depot and 442% at Lowes. For added perspective, at Costco alone, sales increased from 2379 to 20,343 over that one week.

Jackery is looking into what’s behind the massive increase in demand. Clearly, there have been climate-related disasters over the past year, including hurricanes and wildfires. Jackery’s collaboration with the Red Cross helps illustrate the benefits of portable power in emergency response. However, that only partially explains the growth. A related potential explanation is the growing push for household preparedness.  There are reports of at least 17 countries encouraging people to keep three to seven days of food, water and other essentials. Winter storm season, grid strain and rising energy costs could be stoking fears of potential power outages. The US FORTRESS America initiative has also added an emphasis on resilience. Together, these signals may be pushing “preparedness” beyond food and water to include power.

Preparedness is gaining emphasis with power becoming an increasingly important part of being prepared. The fear of “what if” can be a powerful motivator. Having backup power can keep the air handlers working for people’s furnaces. People on well water can keep the pumps running. Backup power can keep refrigerators full of food from spoiling.

Overall, Jackery is the global leader in solar generator sales volume and was named the “World’s No.1 Solar Generator Brand” by Frost & Sullivan. With over 15 years of experience and extensive safety protocols, the brand is well established. For the purchase of a product that manages risks, having a trusted brand is clearly valuable.

Although there has not been a detailed study of the consumer motivations, preparedness is likely a major motivator. However, versatile portable power stations have additional benefits. I keep finding new ways to use the HomePower 1000 Plus V2. And new possible benefits keep opening up.

Beyond providing emergency power, I can take power with me. I can set up an office remotely. I can run and recharge tools away from an outlet. I can power a radiant heater for a few hours while sitting outdoors. I can power an air conditioner for hours or run a fan all day. I can make coffee and cook food. In many ways, the batteries can replace functions once covered not just by a generator, but also a campfire or grill.

While using the battery, I also became more aware of my electricity usage. Seeing how quickly different appliances deplete the battery makes me realize where my utility bill is really going. Some things use less electricity than I anticipated, and some use far more. That awareness helps me to reduce my overall consumption.

And the UPS function can also save delicate equipment, as well as any work on computers and other machinery during a power disruption. I personally would not run a large print on my 3D printer without the backup battery. Providing stable power can extend the lifespan of many expensive devices.

The ability to integrate solar panels provides an additional level of preparedness, allowing the battery to be recharged by the sun when grid power is not available. However, solar can also charge the battery for daily use. While this may not yet be able to feed into the grid without additional equipment, people can reasonably use solar power fed into the battery to replace grid power at the point of use. When the regulations are figured out, balcony solar could expand the possibilities. All this can reduce people’s energy costs.

The battery can provide power when they need it, rather than just when the sun is shining. And when connected to the grid with a time of use (TOU) plan, it can charge when electricity is inexpensive and provide power when it is expensive. The savings from this alone could pay for the battery and start saving people money on their utility bills. And the grid becomes more stable in the process.

If the current battery capacity is not enough, Jackery makes expandible batteries to add more capacity.

In addition, the portable, scalable batteries can form the foundation of a whole home system. With greater utility communication, the added capacity could open up new possibilities for users to benefit while they help stabilize the grid. And they still benefit from the backup power. In addition, after seeing the capabilities, some people may even be inspired to look into going off-grid.

Of course, Jackery is likely not the only company seeing a surge in sales. I hope consumer demand and adoption is rising across the board. With a low barrier to entry and the ability to provide a level of preparedness, sales of portable batteries are likely to continue to grow.

Jackery is actively focused on removing the barriers to entry. Then the benefits of battery backup and portable power can be realized by more people. As more people see the benefits of portable expandable batteries, more people will want them. As more battery capacity is deployed, more applications can become viable. That not only has the ability to make homes more resilient, but also to build a more resilient grid. With the ability to shift consumption through distributed storage, more renewable energy can be utilized.

People who may have bought originally for preparedness will start to realize the broader benefits of their purchase. When people benefit from something, they will tend to rationalize it. This typically works better to change perspectives than trying to start with a rational argument. When people feel the relief of having backup power available for “what if,” they can then expand upon that with greater feelings of independence. Once they personally benefit from the storage that enables greater renewable adoption, they may increase their support for renewable energy. By addressing fears of “what if,” people may open themselves to thinking about “what’s possible.”

Of course, this might just be a temporary sales blip. But it could also be the start of a rapid expansion in home battery use. That could open up a wide range of new possibilities.

Larry lives in Queens, NY, with his wife and cats. #5824. Nissan Will Pay Toyota RAV4 Owners To Trade Their Car For A New Rogue Hybrid

Nissan's very public struggles are well documented, so it shouldn't come as a surprise that the automaker is taking an aggressive stance with its newest and arguably most important model, the Rogue e-Power Hybrid compact crossover. Compact crossover sales account for a massive share of new car sales each year behind only the full-size pickup segment, with heavyweights like the Honda CR-V, Toyota RAV4, Tesla Model Y, and Nissan Rogue all making the list of the top 10 best-selling cars in the U.S. through Q3 of this year. The Rogue comes in at tenth place on that list, but it turns out Nissan isn't messing around when it comes to improving its ranking, as it's now offering a $1,500 trade-in bonus for anyone who trades a 2021-or-newer Toyota RAV4 for a new Rogue Hybrid.

Our friends at CarsDirect got wind of a dealer bulletin that Nissan sent to its dealers announcing the incentive, which was introduced on November 3 and will run through January 4, 2027.

In order to qualify for the $1,500 trade-in bonus, interested shoppers must have a 2021-or-newer Toyota RAV4 that they trade in when purchasing or leasing a 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid. The deal is transferable to members of the same household, and it can be stacked with Nissan's other current offers. Those other offers include a financing deal of 4.9% APR for 60 months, and a lease deal on the west coast where lessees pay $439 per month for 36 months with $4,959 due at signing and a mileage limit of 10,000 miles per year.

Jalopnik's own Andy Kalmowitz sampled the 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid at the first drive event in Santa Barbara, California, late last month which you can check out here, and he preferred driving the new Rogue Hybrid over the new Toyota RAV4 hybrid.

The 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid features a unique series hybrid drivetrain that operates primarily as an EV. The turbocharged 1.5-liter three-cylinder engine under the hood is solely responsible for charging the Rogue's 1.67-kWh battery, and is not connected to the wheels. The wheels are driven by electric motors mounted on the front and rear axles providing standard all-wheel-drive, and they're capable of scooting the Rogue from 0-to-60 in a quick 6.4 seconds without ever needing to be plugged in. It's rated for 41 mpg in the city, 36 mpg on the highway, and 38 mpg combined which is slightly worse than the RAV4 hybrid, but Andy says the Rogue's interior is a much more comfortable and luxurious space than the RAV4 provides.
